sources.title: How Blake Anderson ideates viral single-player apps: big problems, simplicity, and remarkability
sources.originalTitle: How to IDEATE a Viral App in 2025 (1/5)
sources.summary: Blake explains the first step of building viral apps like Rizz GPT, UMax and Cal AI: finding a viral idea. He lays out three principles (solve big problems, keep it simple, make it remarkable) and three methods (scan social media, research the App Store, disconnect to let ideas form).

principles.text: Frame your app as one solution to a big, fundamental problem, not the full solution to a minor one.
principles.quote: your app doesn't have to be the entirety of the solution but if you frame it as one solution to a big problem that people have it will be significantly more viral than framing it as the full solution to a relatively minor problem

principles.text: Simplicity drives virality: you should be able to describe your app in three words and demo it in seconds.
principles.quote: you should be able to describe the unique nature of your app in three words R GPT respond to girls umax face analysis CI photo calorie counter it really is that simple

principles.text: Make the product remarkable: pass the 'did you hear about...' test so users naturally tell friends.
principles.quote: your app needs to be something that people naturally want to tell their friends about did you hear about the AI that can text girls for you did you hear about the app that rates how attractive you are

principles.text: Build shareable moments that trigger emotion; keep iterating on the idea until it does.
principles.quote: your app needs to make people feel something surprise excitement anger anything but in difference

principles.text: Break out of your feed bubble by consuming content outside your demographic to find new problems and ideas.
principles.quote: the key here is breaking out of your bubble your feed is naturally an echo chamber of stuff that you're already interested in New Perspectives means new opportunities means new viral ideas

principles.text: Research the App Store with real download and revenue data, and avoid spaces that are graveyards of failures.
principles.quote: if there's a graveyard of failures and no successes avoid the space entirely the goal here is not to copy it's to identify Market gaps and inefficiencies

sources.title: How to develop a viral app in 2025: mindset, tool stack, and prompting (RizzGPT, UMax, Cal AI)
sources.originalTitle: How to DEVELOP a Viral App in 2025 (3/5)
sources.summary: Blake Anderson explains how he built RizzGPT, UMax and Cal AI. He covers three principles (growth mindset, deep work, progressive overload) and three methods (React Native + Expo in Cursor, managed backend tools, and learning to prompt AI well). The aim is to cut friction from first line of code to millions of users.

principles.text: Treat AI as a tutor and co-pilot, not something that does all the work. Both 'one hour' and 'impossible in a month' claims are lies.
principles.quote: أعتقد أنه من المهم جدًا ألا تنظر إلى الذكاء الاصطناعي على أنه يقوم بكل العمل نيابةً عنك، بل يجب أن تراه كأداة فعالة للغاية ومعلم خاص.

principles.text: Ship a bad first version. It only needs to work; you figure out the rest over time.
principles.quote: نسختك الأولى ستكون سيئة. هذا لا بأس به. كانت النسخة الأولى من "Re GPT" مروعة، لكنها عملت وهذا هو الشيء الوحيد المهم.

principles.text: Do deep work with no distractions. Set a specific goal for each session and execute a plan rather than coding endlessly.
principles.quote: الأمر لا يتعلق بالعمل لساعات أطول. بل يتعلق بجعل ساعات عملك ذات قيمة. حدد أهدافًا محددة لكل جلسة عمل.

principles.text: The worst failure is shipping nothing at all, not shipping bad code.
principles.quote: أكبر فشل قد ترتكبه كمطور ليس إطلاق كود سيء، بل عدم إطلاق أي شيء على الإطلاق لأنك لم تخصص الوقت لإنجاز العمل.

principles.text: Progressive overload: start with the smallest possible feature set, one core input-to-output action, and take on harder projects as your skills grow.
principles.quote: بالنسبة لمنتجك، ابدأ بأقل مجموعة ممكنة من الميزات. تطبيق Riz GPT، ارفع لقطة شاشة، واحصل على استجابة.

principles.text: Let big established platforms handle backend, payments testing and AI instead of building custom infrastructure.
principles.quote: فيما يتعلق بالبنية التحتية للخلفية، هناك الكثير من الإعدادات المخصصة التي يمكنك القيام بها ، لكنني أفضل عموماً ترك المنصات الكبيرة القائمة تتولى المهام الشاقة بدلاً مني.

sources.title: How Blake Anderson markets viral apps: 3 principles and 3 methods (UGC, influencers, ads)
sources.originalTitle: How to MARKET a Viral App in 2025 (4/5)
sources.summary: Blake lays out how he marketed Rizz GPT, UMax and Cal AI to millions of downloads. Principles: do more than you study, sell emotional benefits tied to core human desires, and iterate rapidly. Methods in order of profitability for new founders: internal UGC accounts, influencer partnerships, then paid platform ads.

principles.text: Stop studying and start doing: spend about 80% of time executing and 20% studying and reflecting.
principles.quote: 80% of your time should be spent doing whereas 20% of your time should be spent studying and reflecting and when you do study focus on studying actual case studies rather than just Theory

principles.text: Sell the emotional benefit tied to core human desires, not the feature list.
principles.quote: don't tell me what your app does tell me how it will make my life better

principles.text: Apps go viral by tapping core desires: attraction, status, self-improvement, entertainment.
principles.quote: the most successful apps often tap into core human desires sexual attraction social status self-improvement and entertainment

principles.text: Iterate rapidly and optimize for learning; test many hooks, double down on winners, and don't get attached to any angle.
principles.quote: we tested five to 10 different hookes across our own accounts as well as influencers that we worked with we figured out which ones perform best double down on those

principles.text: Quantity beats perfection: like the pottery class graded on number of pots, make more and learn faster.
principles.quote: When you're marketing a new product you have un limited pots make more learn faster

principles.text: Start with internal UGC: post on company-owned accounts yourself, learn what works, then hire creators to scale and keep the winners.
principles.quote: first study viral Hooks and content in your apps Niche second begin creating content yourself and figuring out what works third use what you have learned to hire ugc creators

sources.title: How Blake Anderson builds viral AI apps: 3 ideas plus his testing, paywall and influencer playbook
sources.originalTitle: 24 year old making $1m/month from AI shares 3 startup ideas
sources.summary: Blake Anderson (Cal AI, Umax, Rizz GPT) explains how he scaled AI mobile apps past $1M/month by pairing new AI functionality with iterative social-media distribution. He shares three app ideas (Career AI, Journal AI, Language AI) and his process for hook testing, influencer relationships, paywalls and competing with incumbents.

principles.text: Ideate by asking which tools will do well on social media, then let virality inform product design.
principles.quote: what are the tools that are going to do well on social media

principles.text: Run virality as an iterative process: split test hooks and positioning across niches and creators, then build a model of what converts.
principles.quote: I'm engaging in a highly iterative process of generating virality from early on and so that means coming up with new hooks figuring out new ways to position the product in terms of who you're marketing to

principles.text: Build personal relationships with influencers instead of using marketplaces or agencies.
principles.quote: What I don't see people talking about is the development of personal relationships with influencers

principles.text: Pair functional value with a shareable output so a useful tool also becomes viral content.
principles.quote: think around the cross between functionality and virality

principles.text: Optimize paywalls for user count over per-user profit; accept lower LTV to dominate the market and boost word of mouth.
principles.quote: I will accept a lower LTV on a per download basis um in exchange for more people being able to use the platform

principles.text: Beat incumbents by out-iterating them: their teams lack aligned incentives, so a hungry small team can win share.
principles.quote: they won't work as hard as us their incentives internally are not aligned to the point where they will be able to iterate and and progress as quickly as us

sources.title: How Blake Anderson built $2.4M+ consumer AI apps with no coding background and tiny creator promos
sources.originalTitle: The 23-year-old That Made $2.4M with His FIRST App
sources.summary: Blake Anderson, 23, built RizzGPT with ChatGPT's help and grew it to about $200K MRR from two $50 creator promos, then repeated the playbook with UMAX and Cali. He covers picking niches, paying for views not followers, shipping fast, and funding a bigger mission (Apex) with early profits.

principles.text: Pay for views and engagement, not follower counts, when buying creator promos.
principles.quote: Followers aren't actually what matters. It's views, right? And engagement.

principles.text: Find a niche where native content already works and slot your app into it as the hook.
principles.quote: We paid $50 for two separate promos. They just made their normal content and put our app in the middle.

principles.text: A simple product solving a clear problem can win; better solution or distribution gives big upside.
principles.quote: when you build something with a very clear use case solving a very clear problem that people have it can be the simplest product of all time

principles.text: Competitors with weak distribution effectively don't exist; don't over-research the market.
principles.quote: if your competition is not known, it's as if they do not exist.

principles.text: Go to extreme lengths for the few high-leverage creators while still running mass outreach.
principles.quote: when there's something you can do that will really lever lever up your efforts, you need to do everything in your power to make that happen.

principles.text: Ship fast from the hip rather than over-optimizing, especially for utility apps.
principles.quote: Big believer in like shoot from the hip, right? Like I think people spend too much time trying to optimize everything that they do.

sources.title: How Blake Anderson built $10M+ with three AI iPhone apps using influencers, UGC and subscriptions
sources.originalTitle: He Made $10M with 3 iPhone Apps
sources.summary: Blake Anderson explains how he taught himself to code with ChatGPT and built Rizz GPT, UMAX and Cal AI into multimillion-dollar apps. He covers finding ideas in heavily monetized niches, validating by living as the customer, and winning through influencer and in-house UGC distribution, plus low-price subscriptions and margins by channel.

principles.text: Short-form platforms are currently solvable distribution: use influencers, UGC and organic accounts to funnel millions to your app.
principles.quote: Tik Tok and Instagram are very solvable right now you can figure out the various influencer strategies the user generated content strategies organic account growth strategies to funnel millions of people to your products

principles.text: A niche already heavily monetized with physical products signals buyers exist and software can solve a problem there.
principles.quote: when you find a niche that's heavily monetized with physical products that's a good indicator that the niche converts it's also a good indicator that you can probably build a software or application to solve a problem within it

principles.text: Validate by becoming the target customer on social media, consuming the niche's content, then building what you'd want.
principles.quote: I'll create an account say Cal and then purely consume nutrition and dieting and calorie counting weightlifting content essentially becoming the target market or Target demographic

principles.text: Iterate ruthlessly on marketing and double down hard once a channel returns profit on time or money invested.
principles.quote: be ruthless about how you iterate try out different strategies and as soon as you find something that is able to produce profitable returns for the company based on the time and or money investment you double down and double down and double down on that

principles.text: Be relentlessly creative reaching influencers; a cold DM isn't enough, so find hidden contact routes and follow up persistently.
principles.quote: I would find that one of them had a Discord link hidden in their Instagram bio or something and I would join that Discord and I would send a message every 10 minutes until the person responded

principles.text: Use subscriptions at lower price points and split-test offers and placements with a paywall tool to lift revenue per download.
principles.quote: being able to test these different offerings and different placements within the app can take you from making x per user that downloads to 1.5 or 2X

sources.title: Blake Anderson: Building Rizz GPT and $10M in iOS apps, now Apex
sources.originalTitle: How He Used Chat GPT To Make $10,000,000
sources.summary: Day-in-the-life with Blake Anderson, who built Rizz GPT, Umax and other iOS apps to about $10M in sales by 23. He covers his distribution engine (influencer marketing), why he codes in intense sprints, how he thinks about long-term vision, and funding Apex from app cash flow.

principles.text: Make influencer marketing the primary distribution engine for consumer apps; it is the most profitable channel.
principles.quote: it's Prim primarily via influencer marketing we also engage in internal ugc user generated content we do paid platform ads So Meta Tik Tok that sort of thing so everything but influencers are our most profitable strategy

principles.text: Seed launch with underrated creators: two small TikTokers at $50 each drove millions of views and hundreds of thousands of downloads.
principles.quote: we build this app I find these two underrated unknown creators on Tik Tok pay them each 50 bucks bang overnight viral 2 million views 4 million views hundreds of thousands of downloads

principles.text: Coding returns are nonlinear: concentrated daily sessions beat spread-out weekly ones.
principles.quote: if you code once a week for 50 weeks you'll have 50 sessions or if you code once a day for 50 days you'll have 50 sessions but you'll see significantly more improvement over the course of those 50 days then you will see over 50 weeks

principles.text: Go all-in on the first product: months of 12-hour days of pure building.
principles.quote: when I built my first application Riz GPT I spent about 12 hours a day for over a month just behind the computer coding only coding that was it

principles.text: Think long-term about impact, not a short-term money target; money is just the resource to fund the vision.
principles.quote: I don't think about business in regards to like how can I make $10 million I think about it in regards to how can I maximize my impact in the footprint that I leave on the world

principles.text: Built apps keep earning; recurring cash flow from past apps can fund the next company.
principles.quote: the thing about these businesses is as you can see like they don't just die like Riz gbt is still doing 200 a month umax is still doing 50 to 400 a month

sources.title: How Blake Anderson built Rizz GPT, UMax and Cal AI with creator-led distribution
sources.originalTitle: The 23-Year-Old Genius Building Million Dollar Apps
sources.summary: Blake walks through three consumer AI utility apps and the playbook behind them: find an untapped social niche, ship a simple app that delivers value, and push it viral with influencer promos. He also covers vetting influencers, making cold outreach unignorable, and why he went big when a copycat appeared.

principles.text: Deliver real value and make it shareable; that is enough to launch a consumer utility app, even if the app is rough.
principles.quote: we provided value to people and we made it viral and in this space that's really all you need to get started

principles.text: Look for an untapped niche on social media and build a tool for the content people already consume there.
principles.quote: we found this Niche this untapped niche of Riz content where people are essentially demonstrating how good they are at talking to girls

principles.text: Most influencers lose money, but a few return 10x; find those and run as many of them as you can to scale.
principles.quote: there exist influencers that can produce 10x rois and if you can run as many of those as possible it's extremely scalable

principles.text: To pick influencers who convert, immerse yourself in the niche content first so you know who the audience actually listens to.
principles.quote: the first thing I did was dive heads down into becoming someone who is obsessed with the content myself

principles.text: Make cold outreach unignorable: follow up across channels and lead with thoughtful value, not mass copy-paste messages.
principles.quote: you have to make yourself unignorable

principles.text: When a copycat threatens you, go big on distribution now rather than wait to perfect the product and lose the market.
principles.quote: I figured it was better to burn through the forest and then pursue this long-term Vision in the future rather than to allow us to be beat in the short term

sources.title: Blake Anderson on building AI apps after Cal AI: chain features, warm-account volume, skills as the bottleneck
sources.originalTitle: This 24-Year-Old Used AI to Make $30M in under a year
sources.summary: Blake Anderson, co-founder of Cal AI (now over $2.5M a month), reflects on a year of wins and failed projects (Apex, the first 10X). He argues one-feature AI apps are saturated, that viral distribution is now a volume game on warmed-up accounts, and that the real bottleneck for builders is personal skill.

principles.text: Becoming technical has never been higher leverage; use AI to code and build, not as a replacement for learning.
principles.quote: I think that there has never been a more high leveraged time to become technical in human history.

principles.text: Single viral AI features are tapped out; chain prompts and steps into fully AI-native products.
principles.quote: People need to stop overindexing on building one key feature that's going to be really viral because most of the really viral one key feature apps have been built.

principles.text: UGC is saturating; the edge is systems that post high volume across many warmed-up accounts.
principles.quote: people that are able to spin up systems of having 100 warm warmed up accounts to which they're posting three videos a day every single day

principles.text: Short-form algorithms follow a power law, so more shots on goal capture outsized upside from the occasional viral hit.
principles.quote: social media algorithms operate as a power law. uh if a video goes viral, there's just this outsized amount of profit that can be earned

principles.text: Kill projects fast when the feedback loop points to no; don't let loops lengthen.
principles.quote: I'm not gonna allow my feedback loops to lengthen and lengthen and lengthen and lengthen when I know that what what the end answer is going to be.

principles.text: With AI levelling capital and hiring, personal skill is the bottleneck; build skills, learn fundamentals, and follow your gut.
principles.quote: The bottleneck for the builders will be how skilled you are.

sources.title: How Blake Anderson built Umax and Rizz GPT to $6M ARR with ChatGPT
sources.originalTitle: How Blake Anderson built a $6 Million app with ChatGPT
sources.summary: Blake explains how he built two consumer AI apps with almost no coding background, using ChatGPT as tutor and code writer. He covers shipping fast, ruthless marketing iteration, betting all revenue on influencers when a copycat appeared, and spotting niches outside the Silicon Valley echo chamber.

principles.text: Ship simple consumer utility apps fast and backfill missing features after launch.
principles.quote: you can learn that [ __ ] along the way the most important thing is just like get your product out there especially when it comes to these sort of consumer utility apps

principles.text: Treat marketing as constant iteration; don't rely on one-size-fits-all channel playbooks.
principles.quote: far and above the most important factor I think in generating some Buzz virality views is a ruthless cycle of iteration just constant iteration testing out new strategies

principles.text: Use ChatGPT as a tutor and coder: describe designs clearly, upload screenshots, paste code, iterate.
principles.quote: it's a lot easier than you think right you just have to start you just have to ask chat GPT

principles.text: Pick co-founders based on gaps in your skills, since complementary decision-making compounds.
principles.quote: what are the gaps here maybe in my skill set that someone else can provide

principles.text: Even if an LLM can do it natively, packaging it as a focused app is still a big opportunity.
principles.quote: just because you can do something natively within the chat GPT app or within any sort of llm does not mean that there is not a massive amount of opportunity to just package it or reskin it

principles.text: Look outside the tech echo chamber; the alpha is in things few people are discussing.
principles.quote: a lot of the alpha Lies when you push past the veil of of the public domain

sources.title: How Blake Anderson built Rizz GPT and UMAX to millions by riding trends with AI
sources.originalTitle: 23 Year Old App Store MILLIONAIRE Used Chat GPT to Get Rich?! (How you can too) | Blake Anderson
sources.summary: Blake Anderson explains how he went from serial teenage side hustles to Rizz GPT (200K downloads, 80K MRR in a week) and UMAX (about $700K in its best month) by spotting a popping TikTok niche, using new AI tech, and buying influencer promos. He covers RPM vs CPM math for influencer deals, why apps are underserved, and why he is shifting to a mission-driven venture.

principles.text: Find a popping niche on social media, then build a product that solves a consumer need in it.
principles.quote: identify a popping niche on TikTok, build a product to solve a consumer need

principles.text: Pair a newly released technology with a trending space to get near-zero competition.
principles.quote: what's a new technology that's enabled uh as a result of recent development, as well as what's a popular space to apply this. And that's where you kind of have zero competition.

principles.text: An influencer promo is profitable when revenue per thousand views, after variable costs, beats cost per thousand views.
principles.quote: any promo that you can run that is going to produce a greater RPM um after your variable cost and whatnot than CPM or the cost for uh per thousand views of that post uh is going to be a profitable one.

principles.text: Influencer marketing is a numbers game; the edge is identifying the few creators whose ads convert, which requires knowing your customer.
principles.quote: you might DM 100 and then 10 will respond three of which might produce profitable ads.

principles.text: When a copycat competitor appears, go all in on marketing immediately and lock up top creators with exclusive contracts.
principles.quote: over the course of about 5 days or sorry, 3 days I deployed a little bit over $200,000 on influencers, which was all the money we had made up until that point.

principles.text: Iterate across many small ventures to build skills, but eventually double down on one to scale.
principles.quote: iteration is very important because you can learn very quickly. But there always comes a time when you need to really double down on your skills, right?

sources.title: How Blake Anderson built viral AI apps: organic content, creator comment sections, and co-founders
sources.originalTitle: From Zero to $30M: How Blake Anderson Built a Viral AI App with No Coding Skills
sources.summary: Blake Anderson explains how he went from kid entrepreneur to launching Rizz GPT, UMax and Cali by packaging new AI tech around core human insecurities and desires. He covers influencer sourcing (take many shots, judge creators by comment sections), content briefs, pricing by channel, co-founder equity, and where he sees opportunity now (AI content, app-to-web, AI hardware).

principles.text: Build products around core human insecurities or desires, not an over-intellectualized use case you then try to make viral.
principles.quote: what my products have really benefited from are taking these core human sort of insecurities or desires and um, orienting a product around that as opposed to figuring out some sort of like overintellectualized use case thing that you're solving and then asking yourself how to make that viral.

principles.text: Being first to market on a new technology makes content inherently viral.
principles.quote: one of the major benefits that my um companies and my apps have benefited from have been being essentially first to market.

principles.text: Take many shots with creators: DM hundreds, don't fixate on a few names.
principles.quote: if you're not DMing hundreds of influencers per day and you're asking yourself why you can't set up partnerships, you're not taking enough shots.

principles.text: Pick creators by engaged comment sections, not follower counts; thoughtful, liked comments signal trust and conversion.
principles.quote: what we really look for are comment sections that it's not just number of comments. It's not just a bunch of fire emojis. It's people responding with um, insights

principles.text: Send every creator a content brief PDF with requirements like early, visible product integration, then approve videos before posting.
principles.quote: content briefs. Content briefs with key information. share that PDF to every creator before they begin making videos.

principles.text: Distribution channel should inform pricing: paid ads suit higher price points, organic suits lower ones.
principles.quote: Organic is usually more conducive to a lower price point. Maybe you do $30 a year, maybe it's $4 a week.

sources.title: How Blake Anderson built UMax from idea to $6M ARR in under 4 months
sources.originalTitle: Why Paperclipmaxx When You Can Looksmaxx? with Blake Anderson
sources.outlet: Emergent Behavior: What's Happening in AI?
sources.summary: Blake Anderson explains how he spotted looksmaxing as the biggest niche in male self-improvement and shipped UMax in about a month. He covers building novel products, split-testing angles, viral features, bootstrapping over VC, and the long-term vision of a "Hims for self-improvement" brand.

principles.text: Find a wedge by scanning social media for the biggest niche where existing information is low quality, then build for it.
principles.quote: I started scanning social media and I was like okay where is there a wedge where's a good place to enter um looks maxing is currently the most popular Niche on social media for young men

principles.text: Embed yourself in the community and think like a user so you build the best product for them.
principles.quote: I need to become one of these people and I need to think like them in order to build the best product for them

principles.text: Build something truly novel, not a 1% improvement on a popular product or a mashup of two. Ideas tried many times and failed are a bad sign.
principles.quote: I think that one of the biggest issues with most application developers is that they make like a 1% Improvement on an already popular product

principles.text: At launch, split test many angles to find what works, then double down on the winners.
principles.quote: I want to test all the different angles that we can uh to to portray this application

principles.text: Build what people organically want to share: package an inherently viral feature so friends tell friends, then go wide on every platform.
principles.quote: we just think about like what is a very inherently viral feature um and how do we package that and display it in a way that people are going to want to share it with other people

principles.text: Bootstrap when profitable: avoid VCs who never built companies and who can block your decisions.
principles.quote: being that we have the money to not be beholden to anybody I think that uh we are in a in a pretty strong position as a company

sources.title: Blake Anderson on building consumer apps: solve real problems, ride new tech, test every channel
sources.originalTitle: How Blake Anderson went from $0 to $73M at 23 |  The Cap Table #6 🧢
sources.summary: Blake Anderson (Cali, UMAX, Riz GPT) joins a short guest segment to explain how he picks consumer app ideas and grows them. He argues for fleshed-out products over single-function gimmicks, using new technology and trend shifts as idea filters, and testing influencer, UGC and paid channels together. The rest of the episode is other hosts and guests.

principles.text: Build a full product around a clear unsolved problem, not a cheeky single-function app.
principles.quote: more sustainable product and growth strategy in my opinion is to identify um a very clear problem that people experience that is either unsolved or poorly solved and then build an amazing product around that.

principles.text: Long-lasting apps tend to be fleshed out, high quality products rather than one-trick tools.
principles.quote: the most long-term successful apps are usually pretty fleshed out, high quality products. They're not cheeky single function products.

principles.text: Pick ideas by asking what new technology now lets you build that you couldn't build last year.
principles.quote: what products can I build today and this year which I could not build last year.

principles.text: Product quality sets your ceiling; distribution and engineering get you to it.
principles.quote: the quality of your product determines what the ceiling of your outcome can look like.

principles.text: Influencer, UGC and paid ads reinforce each other. Try all and double down on what your customers respond to.
principles.quote: there's influencer marketing heavy, there's UGC heavy, and there's paid ads heavy. And I don't think that any of these are mutually exclusive.

principles.text: Hire engineers who ship side projects over those who grind for grades.
principles.quote: I want to hire the CS major that spent all this time building projects and got a mid GPA over the CS major that spent all this time grinding for a good grade.

sources.title: How Blake Anderson scaled AI consumer apps to millions a month (Cal AI, UMAX, RizzGPT)
sources.originalTitle: App Mafia: Young Entrepreneurs Making $3,000,000/Month With AI Apps (Cal AI & Quittr)
sources.summary: Blake Anderson explains how he went from a flopped social app to AI apps doing millions a month by spotting macro trends, copying proven organic dropshipping-style distribution, and bootstrapping. He covers problem selection, marketing with UGC creators, removing user friction, and why VC money isn't the bottleneck.

principles.text: Borrow a proven organic distribution playbook from another niche and apply it to a new product category.
principles.quote: we took the dropshipping um sort of organic content strategy using these sort of underground influencers, UGC, whatever it may be. We applied it to AI apps.

principles.text: Pick the right macro trend and position yourself in it; the upside is far larger than a safe career path.
principles.quote: you just got to understand the macro trends and then position yourself accordingly and the upside is near infinite.

principles.text: Start from problems you or people close to you feel, then study what competing apps do and build a solution for a specific pain point.
principles.quote: find the problems that you or the people close to you experience do the market research, identify the key pain points, and then look at what other apps in similar industries do

principles.text: Marketing is a simple loop: find creators, test UGC hooks, publish, and double down on what works.
principles.quote: marketing is as simple as identify the correct creators, identify the correct hooks for UGC, create the content, put it out into the world, and continue to iterate um and double down on what works

principles.text: Remove friction so users stay committed to the goal; accept good-enough accuracy over perfection that causes them to quit.
principles.quote: we remove the friction and we increase the probability that they're going to stay committed to the goal.

principles.text: Cash isn't the bottleneck in consumer apps; industry insight and agency are, so bootstrapping works and VC is for much bigger outcomes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake explains the first step of building viral apps like Rizz GPT, UMax and Cal AI: finding a viral idea. He lays out three principles (solve big problems, keep it simple, make it remarkable) and three methods (scan social media, research the App Store, disconnect to let ideas form).

chunks.heading: Core principle: a viral idea minimizes friction from inception to millions of users
chunks.text:
- Blake defines a viral idea as "one that minimizes the amount of friction from inception to millions of users."
- He focuses on single-player utility apps: no complex backend, no social or fun functionality required.
- The idea sets the foundation for design, development and distribution. A bad idea wastes time on everything downstream.
- Example: Blake says the execution on Rizz GPT "was not great at all," but it had a viral idea, and that made everything else "10 times easier."
- His track record: three apps (Rizz GPT, Umax, Cal AI) that each generated millions of downloads and millions in profit in one year.

chunks.heading: Principle 1: solve big problems
chunks.text:
- People want solutions to big problems they actually have. He cites Maslow's hierarchy of needs: nobody cares about feeling part of a group if there is no food on the table.
- Solve the most fundamental problems. His apps map to them: Rizz GPT helps you get more girls, Umax helps you become more attractive, Cal AI helps you reach fitness goals.
- Biological imperative: life exists to continue living and to reproduce, so help people with those things.
- The app does not need to be the entire solution. Framing it as one solution to a big problem is significantly more viral than framing it as the full solution to a relatively minor problem.

chunks.heading: Principle 2: more complicated means less viral
chunks.text:
- Virality is contingent on simplicity. Even if the app is framed as the answer to getting more girls, a 25-step path to get there kills interest.
- Test: you should be able to describe the app's unique nature in three words.
  - Rizz GPT: "respond to girls"
  - Umax: "face analysis"
  - Cal AI: "photo calorie counter"
- Simplicity affects every part of growth:
  - How easily people understand the app.
  - How likely they are to tell friends.
  - How quickly it can be demonstrated in content.
- On TikTok you have about 3 seconds to capture attention. If the app is too complicated to show in that window, "you're fighting an uphill battle."
- Formula: simple concepts, simple execution, massive growth.

chunks.heading: Principle 3: the "did you hear about..." test (make it remarkable)
chunks.text:
- The app must be something people naturally want to tell friends about. If you can't fill in "Did you hear about the app that ___?" naturally, growth will be a struggle.
  - "...the AI that can text girls for you?"
  - "...the app that rates how attractive you are?"
  - "...the app that lets you count calories just with pictures?"
- How his apps spread:
  - Rizz GPT: screenshots posted in TikTok content.
  - Umax: people sharing transformations and before/after ratings.
  - Cal AI: people showing off their meals and macros.
- The app needs to create moments worth sharing. Gut-checks:
  - Would someone bring it up at a party?
  - Would someone text their mom about it?
  - Would someone send it to a group chat?
- It should make people feel something (surprise, excitement, anger), "anything but indifference." When Blake first built Umax and pulled it out at a party, everybody wanted to find out what they were rated.
- If the app doesn't create these moments, keep iterating on the idea until it does. "The most viral products aren't just useful, they are remarkable."

chunks.heading: Method 1: scan social media (non-negotiable)
chunks.text:
- Social media is "a manifestation of the collective conscious": what people are interested in and talking about.
- He says there is no magic bullet for spotting new trends, but he:
  - Uses Google Trends to see what's popping off.
  - Explores Reddit communities.
  - Reads comment sections on Instagram, TikTok and other platforms.
- Next level: create new accounts and consume content you would never normally engage with. Example: a 25-year-old guy who watches weightlifting and programming content makes an account for what a 35-year-old mom would watch (family cooking, interior design, pickleball). "You'll be amazed with parts of the internet that you never knew existed."
- How this led to Umax: he saw one thing about looksmaxing that piqued his interest, then made accounts dedicated entirely to looksmaxing content. He figured out which forums they lived on and what products they used, and eventually learned exactly what problems these people had, which let him build a product around it.
- Key point: break out of your bubble. Your feed is an echo chamber of what you already like. New perspectives mean new opportunities and new viral ideas.

chunks.heading: Method 2: research the App Store
chunks.text:
- Don't just browse; discover what works and what doesn't.
- Process:
  - Download a new app every day.
  - Watch the content the app posts on social media and work out why it is or isn't succeeding.
  - Look up the app on Sensor Tower for monthly downloads and monthly revenue, because your first guess about whether an app is succeeding isn't necessarily right.
- Example: before building Cal AI, he downloaded every calorie tracker he could find and asked whether there was really opportunity, looking for shortcomings and room for improvement.
- Avoid graveyard spaces: if an idea has been tried 100 times with no successes, stay away. Examples: social weightlifting apps, and a college marketplace (the first app he ever tried, which fell victim to this).
- The goal is not to copy but to find market gaps and inefficiencies. A problem across the industry that nobody has solved may be an opportunity.

chunks.heading: Method 3: disconnect to let ideas form
chunks.text:
- The best ideas don't come when forced; they come in moments of clarity. He recommends long walks with no phone, no music, nothing.
- Where his ideas came from: Rizz GPT on a walk home, Umax on a hike.
- Social media and app research are inputs. The mind needs time to produce outputs, like a computer clearing memory.
- Most founders consume content 24/7 (X, tech articles, TikTok), leaving no space for original thought. That is why everybody builds the same things: everyone saw ChatGPT and built AI chatbots; everyone saw Stable Diffusion and built AI avatar generators.
- Real viral opportunities require synthesis, connecting dots others haven't:
  - Male dating frustration + AI led to Rizz GPT.
  - Looksmaxing community problems + AI vision led to Umax.
  - Calorie-counting friction + computer vision led to Cal AI.
- These connections happen in the shower, on walks and during workouts. "The greatest founders aren't necessarily the smartest, they're the ones that dare to think differently from the rest."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson explains how he built RizzGPT, UMax and Cal AI. He covers three principles (growth mindset, deep work, progressive overload) and three methods (React Native + Expo in Cursor, managed backend tools, and learning to prompt AI well). The aim is to cut friction from first line of code to millions of users.

chunks.heading: Mindset: Build Fast Without Faking It
chunks.text:
- Blake says anyone claiming you can build a working app "in an hour with AI" is lying. He says anyone claiming you can't go from zero to a fully working app in a month with AI is lying too: "the truth lies somewhere in between."
- The biggest barrier for beginners is mindset, not technical skill. He built RizzGPT with almost no coding experience, using AI as a teacher and personal assistant rather than something that does all the work.
- Growth mindset: don't get discouraged if it takes longer than an hour, but push to move as fast as possible and reject the idea that building will take a year. Start today even if you're not ready, and you'll figure it out over time.
- Expect a bad first version. The first RizzGPT was "horrendous," but it worked, "and that's the only thing that matters."
- Blake counts himself as the first person to build three different mobile apps (RizzGPT, UMAX, Cal AI) that each reached millions in revenue and millions of downloads in one year. He focuses on single-service apps with no social features and no complex backend.

chunks.heading: Deep Work: Block Time and Ship
chunks.text:
- Building needs focused, uninterrupted time. People used to social media often struggle moving from fast-moving feeds to deep, isolated work.
- Example: block 4 hours of deep work for coding with no phone, no email, no distractions. Just you, the code editor, some AI, and Stack Overflow.
- It's about making hours count, not working more hours. Set a specific goal per session, such as:
  - Build the camera interface.
  - Finish onboarding.
  - Add a paywall.
- Don't code endlessly. Make a plan and execute it.
- Apps fail not because of bad code but because nothing ships. "The biggest failure you can make as a developer isn't shipping bad code, it's not shipping any code at all."

chunks.heading: Progressive Overload: Start Small, Scale Up
chunks.text:
- Like lifting weights, increase difficulty gradually, both in your product and your skills.
- Product: launch with the smallest possible feature set.
  - RizzGPT: upload a screenshot, get a response.
  - UMAX: upload a face photo, get ratings.
  - Cal AI: upload a food photo, get calories.
- Skills: start with easy apps. Had Blake started with UMAX or Cal AI, they would have taken at least twice as long as RizzGPT, and he might never have finished.
- Add features and take on harder projects over time. A bug that takes 10 hours at first may take 5, then 3, then 2, then the 1 hour it should take.
- Loop: "Build, launch, learn."

chunks.heading: Tech Stack Recommendation for 2025
chunks.text:
- Frontend: React Native with Expo, built in Cursor.
  - React Native is the core framework, Expo simplifies the workflow, and Cursor is the best AI code editor.
  - Lets you build for iOS and Android at once, ship updates quickly, and use AI to speed development.
  - Blake started with SwiftUI, but if he started today he would use this stack.
- Priority is learning the frontend and shipping as fast as possible. His bias: "execute first, learn second." If you're already a developer on another stack, that's fine; this is the best stack for beginners in 2025.

chunks.heading: Backend and Tooling
chunks.text:
- Blake says he's not a backend expert and speaks from his own experience and what he's seen successful apps do. He prefers letting big established platforms handle the heavy lifting rather than heavy custom setups.
- Supabase or Firebase: handle user authentication, databases, file storage, API endpoints and more.
- Superwall: for testing paywalls and monetization. It lets you A/B test paywalls and offers at different points in the app with different designs, in real time.
- AI features: use Anthropic (Claude) or OpenAI (ChatGPT) APIs. Read their documentation to understand how the endpoints work.
- Keep up with the latest AI capabilities to improve existing features or create entirely new ones.

chunks.heading: Prompting AI Effectively
chunks.text:
Blake calls prompting probably the most important skill of the future, beyond app development.

- Be specific and structured. Break complex tasks into smaller ones. Without examples of what you want, AI has to guess, like working with another human.
- Iterate and refine. Short feedback loops (as in marketing) let you learn fast what works. Try different ways of talking to the AI and explaining what you want.
- Save your prompts. He keeps different prompts for code generation (with formatting preferences for a given project) and for content scripts. Build an arsenal across AI development, content creation, marketing and ideation.
- Example of a vague vs. specific prompt for an initial layout:
  - Vague: "Can you build an app where I upload a screenshot and it gives me responses for girls?"
  - Specific: one button in the center reading "Upload screenshot," white text inside, red outline around it; tapping it opens the photo library to pick an image, which then calls the OpenAI API.
  - He then iterates back and forth until the structure matches what he wants, and remembers (or saves) the prompting techniques that worked best.
- "AI is a co-pilot, not an autopilot." The better and clearer your instructions, the more value you get. It takes time to learn, but it's likely the best investment you can make in yourself.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake lays out how he marketed Rizz GPT, UMax and Cal AI to millions of downloads. Principles: do more than you study, sell emotional benefits tied to core human desires, and iterate rapidly. Methods in order of profitability for new founders: internal UGC accounts, influencer partnerships, then paid platform ads.

chunks.heading: Start doing: Blake's 80/20 rule against analysis paralysis
chunks.text:
- Blake says founders stuck in "endless research and studying and devising the perfect launch strategy" never launch. Studying marketing without doing it gets you nowhere.
- Spend 80% of your time doing and 20% studying and reflecting. When you study, use real case studies, not theory.
- He has "never purchased a course on marketing in my entire life". The best marketers he knows didn't learn from courses.
- The loop is: try, fail, succeed, analyze what worked and what didn't. This applies to any domain.
- He rebuts three common excuses:
  - "I need to learn more first": you learn by doing.
  - "I don't want to waste money": you can create free content yourself.
  - "I don't know any creators": start DMing them.
- His own first attempts failed too. The answer to failing is to keep getting shots up, not to study more.

chunks.heading: Marketing the emotional benefit, not the features
chunks.text:
- Blake defines marketing at its most primitive as understanding how people think and what motivates them, then using that to capture attention.
- The most successful apps tap core desires: sexual attraction, social status, self-improvement and entertainment.
- His examples:
  - Rizz GPT went viral by tapping people's desire to be charismatic with members of the opposite sex.
  - Umax went viral because it validates how attractive people think they are.
  - Cal AI went viral because it helps people reach their fitness goals.
- Marketing should focus on the emotional benefit and the problem solved, not features: "don't tell me what your app does tell me how it will make my life better".
- His context is single-player utility apps: apps that solve a problem and need no complex backend. Viral marketing aims to minimize friction between launch and millions of users.

chunks.heading: Rapid iteration: test many hooks and let data decide
chunks.text:
- The goal is to optimize for learning until you find scalable strategies.
- Umax example: early on he wrote a list of hooks and tested 5 to 10 across the company's own accounts and across influencers.
  - "POV you use the Umax app to glow up": a creator shows a side-by-side of face ratings before and after, for example 55 to 95.
  - "Here are the best haircuts for your face shape": creators scan their face and show the recommended haircut in the app.
- They doubled down on the winners. This took Umax to over $600,000 in monthly revenue within 3 months.
- He says that even though he's good at marketing, he can't come up with a hook that works every time. Don't get emotionally attached to any single angle; let the data guide you.
- Pottery class story: one class had a whole semester to make a single best pot, the other was graded on the number of pots. The quantity class made better pots too, by learning through trial and error. When marketing a new product "you have unlimited pots", so make more and learn faster.

chunks.heading: Method 1: Internal UGC (most profitable, least scalable, best place to start)
chunks.text:
- Internal UGC is content created and posted to company-owned accounts. It is the most profitable way to market an app and the best starting point with little to no capital.
- Rizz GPT example:
  - Tens of accounts were named things like "get Rizz GPT" or "Rizz GPT app".
  - It started with the main account, now named Plug AI, run by his co-founders Alex and Evan.
  - They began with video demos of the app, then shifted quickly to Rizz slideshow content. In the first month of that shift the account alone generated nearly 50 million views.
- Once winning strategies were known, they hired teams of UGC creators to run accounts. Four of five of those accounts flopped, but one produced a 20x return.
- Process:
  1. Study viral hooks and content in your app's niche.
  2. Start creating content yourself and figure out what works.
  3. Use what you learned to hire UGC creators to run their own accounts and scale it. Retain those who do well and replace those who don't.

chunks.heading: Method 2: Influencer partnerships (very scalable, hard to do right)
chunks.text:
- This is the next most profitable way to scale. Blake says you should probably study psychology and statistics to get good at it, and he plans future videos on it.
- Finding influencers:
  - You need a strong understanding of the content and influencers in your niche.
  - "If I DM'd 10 influencers and nobody responded", the answer is that you need to DM hundreds.
  - Once you work with them, ask them to refer you to other creators they know.
- Pricing:
  - Pay based on average view count. A creator averaging 100,000 views might get roughly $100 to $1,000 depending on niche.
  - A contract (for example 4 posts per month) is usually much cheaper than one-off videos.
- Vetting: analyze the comment section. An engaged, largely American audience is a good sign. A comment section full of bot accounts leaving fire emojis will not convert.
- Attribution:
  - Direct attribution for organic social is "currently next to impossible".
  - Instead, watch your app's conversion dashboard and the influencer's post in real time, and assess how well views convert into downloads and purchases.
  - Build an intuitive understanding of each creator and how well they convert.

chunks.heading: Method 3: Platform ads (most scalable, lowest profit share, needs capital)
chunks.text:
- Platform ads are the most scalable method but the least profitable as a percentage of revenue, and they need the most upfront capital. Blake would not prioritize them for a new app developer.
- Main channels: Meta, TikTok, Google and Apple Search.
- Steps:
  1. Compile a large number of creatives: a mix of videos and images, in different content styles covering every angle you can market the app from.
  2. Install the necessary SDKs for attribution.
  3. Run campaigns with small budgets first to find winning creatives and ad strategies, then scale up.
- Ads work best for apps with high LTV (a lot of money per user). Low-LTV apps work better through organic marketing, which is why he recommends UGC and influencer partnerships for people getting started.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson (Cal AI, Umax, Rizz GPT) explains how he scaled AI mobile apps past $1M/month by pairing new AI functionality with iterative social-media distribution. He shares three app ideas (Career AI, Journal AI, Language AI) and his process for hook testing, influencer relationships, paywalls and competing with incumbents.

chunks.heading: Background and credibility
chunks.text:
- Blake Anderson was 23 at the time. He "stumbled into" the AI mobile app space a little over a year earlier.
- His apps:
  - Riz GPT (now Plug AI): a little over 3M downloads, about $200K monthly revenue.
  - Umax: over 10M downloads, about $500K monthly revenue now (closer to $400K), peaking around $700K/month.
  - Cal AI: launched a little over 6 months before the interview, about 2M downloads, over $1M monthly revenue.
- He is launching a new content-heavy company called Apex.
- His thesis: the space sits at the intersection of new AI functionality and novel distribution tactics pioneered by e-commerce people. A small group of 18 to 22 year olds runs it.
- AI lets you deliver personalized functionality updated in real time. It also lets you build things that used to need costly proprietary tech. Umax's facial analysis used GPT Vision with essentially zero upfront development cost beyond his own time.

chunks.heading: Iterative virality and influencer relationships
chunks.text:
- Don't bet everything on one trendy way to go viral. Run a highly iterative process from early on:
  - Come up with new hooks and new positioning for who you market to.
  - Split test them continuously across niches, videos and creators.
  - Track views per hook and conversion per view. Over time this builds a mental or real statistical model that informs distribution.
- This is the same approach Meta and TikTok apply to creatives, applied to influencers, in-house UGC and hook generation.
- Example for a career app: find ed-tech, study-tip, job-application and productivity influencers. Write different hooks per niche and test them across creators.
- He does not use influencer marketplaces, databases or agencies. He calls the messaging that you should "outright wrong".
- What he does instead is build personal relationships with influencers:
  - They get hundreds of DMs and emails daily and can't tell serious companies from unserious ones.
  - Once you're embedded in the industry, they connect you to whoever you need.
  - Creators like Sam Zia (220K followers), Dawson Gibbs (170K) and Carter (280K) comment on his posts without being paid.
- To solve the cold start, prioritize both quantity and quality early:
  - Reach out to thousands of creators.
  - For a creator you really want, DM them on every platform, "message their mom," message their girlfriend.
  - Then treat them well and become friends.

chunks.heading: Turning an idea into a product
chunks.text:
- Ideation starts with virality: which tools in the product will do well on social media? That informs the design.
- For Umax, the six-factor rating system drew the most likes, comments and engagement, so it went viral.
- With an all-in-one product, split test product hooks too. For example, test three tools on social to see which goes most viral and engineer around it.
- Design process:
  - Make wireframes.
  - Have a professional designer or an Upwork freelancer turn them into fleshed-out UI.
  - Then build.
- Building:
  - He used ChatGPT to teach him to code Riz GPT and the first Umax, starting with SwiftUI and pasting code into Xcode.
  - He now codes in Cursor with React Native, a month in.
  - He did not code Cal AI.
  - If you have capital or a great CTO, he says you don't need to code yourself. There is no one-size-fits-all answer.
- Blend functionality with virality. Take a functional feature and make it shareable, e.g. a six-factor score for each section of a resume.

chunks.heading: Idea 1: Career AI
chunks.text:
- Career tools today are fragmented: resume analyzers, personality-based career quizzes, application courses. Combine them into one app.
- Pricing: about $50 a month for an all-in-one tool "feels pretty obvious."
- Why it works: universities sell themselves as setting you up for a career, and finding jobs and internships is hard.
- Features:
  - Resume analysis with a six-factor score per section, designed around popular ed-tech content and shared via ed-tech creators.
  - Career quiz ending in a shareable result screen.
  - A trend such as seniors getting recommended computer science and asking why it took until senior year to realize they shouldn't study it.
- Distribution: Instagram Reels and TikTok aimed at students, plus Twitter/X and LinkedIn as relatively untapped channels.

chunks.heading: Idea 2: Journal AI and idea 3: Language tutoring AI
chunks.text:
- **Journal AI:**
  - An "AI second brain" framed as a journal, with memory storage and a UI built for journaling.
  - Analysis covers productivity, emotional support and relationship analysis.
  - It need not be technically robust: essentially ChatGPT with more complex memory and a journaling-friendly UI.
  - Thesis: people already use ChatGPT as a journal. Journals give nothing back, and this returns objective analysis.
  - Brand it as a journal, not a therapist. He might name it something friendlier like "Juny" or "Journey".
- **Language AI:**
  - Compete with Duolingo by integrating new AI functionality faster and building a dynamic UI instead of static modules.
  - Voice model costs are high now but he expects them to fall.
  - Learners are high-intent. Taking about 1% of a roughly $1B market would be a $100M app.
  - His answer to "Duolingo will build this": incumbents' incentives aren't aligned. Cal AI heard the same about MyFitnessPal, whose engineers and social media managers probably hold little equity after repeated sales.
  - Cal AI's calorie estimates from images are significantly better than MyFitnessPal's, and it pioneers new social marketing.
  - Few people try to beat entrenched players, which makes it easier to succeed with these tactics.
  - Frame it as an app that tutors through its UI, not as an "AI tutor."

chunks.heading: Naming and the "AI" suffix
chunks.text:
- Appending AI helps when innovating in a stagnant industry (Cal AI in calorie tracking), where AI signals sophistication.
- Skip it where accuracy is critical, such as a medical document service, because people may fear errors.
- His co-founder Zach tweeted that adding AI is a negative signal. They resolved it with the distinction above.
- Cal AI is the name he's proudest of.
- Umax was named for a planned all-in-one self-improvement ecosystem. In retrospect, with that plan he'd have called it "looksmax AI," as a copycat did.
- Naming is not his strength; he points to others for that.

chunks.heading: Paywalls and pricing
chunks.text:
- He uses Superwall (not affiliated) and no longer uses RevenueCat. It makes split testing easy and gives all the data.
- Most of the industry optimizes users multiplied by profit per user. He optimizes users raised to a power greater than one, multiplied by profit per user.
- He accepts lower LTV per download for more people using the product. Reasons:
  - Dominate the market faster.
  - Increase word of mouth, which is nearly impossible to measure once you run ads constantly.
- Standard industry practice: take users through an onboarding flow (quiz, push notification permission, personal info "to customize the app") and hit them with the paywall at the end. It converts far better than other placements, and he has done this on his apps.
- He's ambivalent about the ethics ("I don't feel good about it"). He argues it doesn't move the needle much and that the money funds what he's building.

chunks.heading: Finding more app ideas
chunks.text:
- Use Sensor Tower to size the other players in a space.
- Hike or walk, where he thinks clearly.
- Deliberately scroll social media with burner accounts curated to one topic. When building Umax, the account had only looksmaxxing content. Put yourself in the mind of the content's consumer.
- Obvious ideas are often best: calorie tracking, language learning, journaling. He rates them "10 out of 10" because they're nearly impossible to fail with.
- Riz GPT was a 10 out of 10 for a first small win, with a lower ceiling.
- Follow the new styles of execution, build functionality and distribution, and build small MVPs rather than boiling the ocean.
- He planned a free 30 to 60 minute course or video and a free "viral app Playbook" PDF, shared via his socials (Blake Anderson on X, Apex on Instagram).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson, 23, built RizzGPT with ChatGPT's help and grew it to about $200K MRR from two $50 creator promos, then repeated the playbook with UMAX and Cali. He covers picking niches, paying for views not followers, shipping fast, and funding a bigger mission (Apex) with early profits.

chunks.heading: Blake's first app: RizzGPT, from idea to $200K MRR
chunks.text:
- Blake had only basic Python experience and had never built software. He got hooked on ChatGPT in late 2022 and graduated college around mid-2023 without wanting a full-time job.
- The idea came from a roommate who kept asking what to say to girls on dating apps. Blake pasted the transcript into ChatGPT, found the replies robotic, and spent time prompt-engineering them to "sound like a human and have Rizz."
- The product: upload a screenshot of your messages, OCR pulls out the conversation (left side is her, right side is you), the GPT API generates reply options, and you copy-paste them. A "spice meter" makes replies more flirtatious.
- His thesis for all three of his apps: "Guys don't know how to text girls." Guys already send these screenshots in group chats, so the product is the same behavior moved into an app.
- Results: a couple hundred downloads in the first weeks, then about $80K monthly revenue right after launch, scaling to a little over $200K MRR, held steady for about 10 months. Total revenue was heading toward $2.5M.
- Pricing: free at first, with credits, then $7 a week. Later it was a flat $7 a week.

chunks.heading: How $100 of promos drove 200K downloads
chunks.text:
- Blake found a niche on social media: "Rizz content," where guys show off conversations with girls in 10-image slideshows. Those creators had roughly 50K to 100K followers but got millions of views per video.
- He paid $50 each for two promos. The creators made their normal content and worked the app into the middle. Those two videos got a few million views each, nearly 200,000 downloads in under a week, and about $80K in monthly revenue.
- Why it converts: the creator shows the conversations working, then credits the app. It works like Michael Jordan saying "wear my shoes." The viewer sees the outcome and thinks the app is the missing piece.
- Views and engagement matter, not followers. He says "washed up" creators with millions of followers can get 20K views a video, and brands that pay per follower are using the wrong strategy.
- Promos were cheap because the niche was new. Few other advertisers could monetize Tinder-message content. His rule is to find the audience that converts best, where you have the most comparative advantage, and double down.
- He did not use affiliate deals, because attribution on mobile apps is messy. Streetwear-style checkout codes don't work for apps.

chunks.heading: Influencer outreach tactics
chunks.text:
- It is a numbers game and a quality game at once. Reach out to hundreds of creators a day, but go to extremes for the few you really need.
- For one key creator he joined the creator's Discord, spammed hourly, and messaged the creator's mom and girlfriend (politely, e.g. "would love to pay your son to do some work for me"). His rule: when something would greatly lever your efforts, do everything in your power to make it happen.
- Most people who say "I DM'd 20 influencers and nobody replied" spent about 20 minutes. He says you have to put in the time.
- The message has to be split-tested like ad copy, and there is no universal template. RizzGPT, UMax and Cali each needed a different approach.
- In noisy niches, be direct: "Love your content. Looking to pay you X dollars for a promo. Let me know if you're interested." Creators are flooded with high-ticket sales pitches.
- Showing value up front (an example video, a redesign) beats a calendar link.
- Influencer marketing is the hardest channel to crack. Most people run unprofitable promos because they take the first creator who says yes and judge by follower or view counts without checking how loyal the audience is. He is skeptical of anyone selling a course on it: "DM people... you have to iterate."

chunks.heading: Building with ChatGPT, no technical background
chunks.text:
- He asked ChatGPT "how do I build a mobile app?", got options (SwiftUI, Kotlin, React Native), and picked SwiftUI. He downloaded Xcode, designed in Figma with a co-founder, and built piece by piece: "I need a blue gradient background... I need two buttons... after this button I need to open the camera roll."
- ChatGPT wrote about 95% of RizzGPT's code and about 90% of UMax's. He debugged by pasting errors back and asking why the code failed. Over time ChatGPT became a tutor, and he asked it to explain concepts.
- The first version took a little over a month. He says he could now build it in a day or two.
- Early mistakes: no backend, no user authentication, API calls made from the front end (so the key was stealable), the app named "RizzGPT-production" on the home screen, and a Heroku backend he'd now replace with AWS.
- Advice: keep pushing through small blocks that cost 20 hours (they cost three minutes later). This works for single-function utility apps; he doesn't think a beginner could build a social app with ChatGPT.
- App Store setup was not a hurdle: set up an LLC and a developer account.
- Weak product ideas have no guarantee (he cites a water-reminder app). A simple product with a clear problem and better solution or distribution has "massive upside."

chunks.heading: Ignoring competition and shooting from the hip
chunks.text:
- Blake didn't know a competitor (the Rizz app) existed when he built RizzGPT. They had under 200K downloads, which RizzGPT matched in its first week. They threatened a lawsuit, which is why the product was renamed Plug AI.
- His view: "If your competition is not known, it's as if they do not exist." A product only exists in society once people know about it, and weak distribution makes a competitor irrelevant.
- He doesn't run focus groups or five-month beta periods: "I build the app, I put it on the market and I hope that it works."
- Exception: consumer social apps, where a weak first impression churns users permanently. For utility apps, being slightly optimized at launch is enough.
- A tell for good ideas: on projects that succeeded, he grew more confident as he thought them through. When his confidence dropped, they didn't work out.
- He thinks through direction first (long walks in the woods with no phone), then builds fast.

chunks.heading: UMax: picking the niche and building it
chunks.text:
- After leaving RizzGPT (amicably, keeping equity and payouts), he spent November 2023 on friends' couches with no money, scrolling social media for what was popping.
- He picked "looksmaxing." Weightlifting content seemed to be declining while looksmaxing was growing (rising on Google Trends). He argued it cuts straight to what lifting was a step away from: being more attractive to girls.
- He researched on Reddit, TikTok and Instagram and found two needs: personalized advice (skincare, hair, grooming) and a way to quantify how attractive you are and track progress.
- Timing: the GPT Vision API was about to be released. A custom facial-analysis ML model would have cost $50K to $100K with no guarantee of quality, while GPT Vision cost under a cent an image. He tweeted that people would make millions off GPT Vision.
- Product: upload a photo and get a rating out of 10, a "potential score" if you improve changeable traits, and recommendations (skincare, hairstyle, grooming, jawline trainers, chewier food, losing weight). He deliberately excluded unchangeable traits like cheekbones, citing an "internal locus of control."
- Scoring method: have the model classify 20+ traits (acne, skin discoloration, grooming, hair vs. face shape, eye bags, jawline strength) and deduct points from a perfect 10 for each issue found. He says GPT does poorly at giving numeric scores directly (every jawline gets about 70) but classifies well.
- Partner: he brought on Sam Zia, a looksmaxing influencer (200K TikTok followers, but 1M+ views a video), plus his older brother. He picked Sam because the community is tight-knit and led by a few creators. He decided partnerships depend on the niche: looksmaxing had a handful of leaders, while calorie tracking has no single leader.
- He also refused practices that would have raised retention and revenue, such as pushing hard into the female beauty niche or excessive subscription pricing.
- Revenue: about $100K in month one, about $200K in month two, then a viral spike to over $500K a month. Total was a little over $3M, with UMax projected to pass $5M in 2024.

chunks.heading: Cali, the studio model, and the team playbook
chunks.text:
- While UMax boomed, Blake gave his calorie-tracking idea, designs, playbook and capital to two 17-year-old founders (Zach and Henry) on an even split. They built it and ran social media. Cali did over $300K in a month, about $3M ARR (not all of it recurring).
- He walked away from UMax's $500K a month because he can't make himself work on things he isn't passionate about. He estimates he gets far less out of the hours he puts in. He calls UMax a "local maximum" that he could break through but doesn't want to.
- Studio model: always keep about 20 app ideas in the back pocket and work the best one. Bring in engineers to lead individual apps, supply designs, infrastructure, paid ads, in-house content and influencer deals.
- Team structure: he sees 2x or better outcomes when two skilled people work on the same app, as long as the ceiling is not low. Split ownership across engineering, design/product/App Store, and marketing.
- Consumer apps allow rapid iteration on distribution, design and engineering, unlike e-commerce, where you wait weeks for samples.
- Distribution varies by app: paid platform ads, influencers, or in-house UGC. He has seen people succeed with each.
- You can tell you've hit a ceiling when you do everything right and growth plateaus.

chunks.heading: Apex: the long-term vision and his philosophy on money
chunks.text:
- Apex is an "all-in-one self-actualization ecosystem" aimed at health, meaning and virtue rather than "get jacked, make 10K a month, buy a Rolex." He frames the position as the opposition to social media's mimetic desire (copying what others want), noting that opposing a prevalent narrative can build a strong community.
- Plan: a content house between San Diego and LA, a founding team including his older brother and Jesse Abed, creator-style content, and free apps (personalized fitness, nutrition and skill plans) and free communities. He will put in at least a couple million of his own money, and he plans to file as a benefit corporation so he can act for the public good instead of maximizing shareholder value.
- His split of earnings: about two-fifths to Apex, two-fifths to his parents, one-fifth to himself.
- He thinks the consumer app space is dominated by LTV maximization and wants to build tools free to use. Monetization (e.g. physical products) is a later question. He compares the brand to FaZe Clan and Barstool, but says he's a "businessman first, creator second."
- On picking pursuits: choose things you care about, so you come out ahead even if you fail. Making money in something you're not proud of (his example: OnlyFans management) means you fail or succeed at a cost. He would rather change a million lives and make zero dollars than make millions and change none.
- On motivation: working on what you love produces far more output per hour, because the subconscious keeps working on it. Time in nature (he cites a study in Cal Newport's *Deep Work*) improves thinking.
- Background: his father had a neurodegenerative condition and the family had financial hardship, with Blake's brother lending him grocery money after college. Blake started investing at seven by tracking MSFT and INTC from the Wall Street Journal, and wrote an ebook at seven called "How to Make Money as a Seven-Year-Old." He says he asked "why" a lot as a kid, and that thinking like everyone else produces the same ideas and results.
- Contact: Blake Anderson on Instagram and Twitter, blakeex.inc, apex.improve.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson explains how he taught himself to code with ChatGPT and built Rizz GPT, UMAX and Cal AI into multimillion-dollar apps. He covers finding ideas in heavily monetized niches, validating by living as the customer, and winning through influencer and in-house UGC distribution, plus low-price subscriptions and margins by channel.

chunks.heading: Building iOS apps with AI: ideas, validation, and the marketing engine behind three apps
chunks.text: Blake taught himself to code with ChatGPT in May and June 2023 and launched his first app in July 2023. He has since built or co-founded three AI apps. Rizz GPT is an AI dating assistant that reached about $2.2M in annual revenue. Umax is an AI looksmaxxing app that did almost $5M in revenue in a year. Cal AI, co-founded with two partners who run operations, did over $1M per month in revenue within about six months of launch. Blake came up with the Cal AI idea and helped with designs, but did not build the app. He set himself a goal right after college of making $50,000 on his own within 12 months, while broke and living at home.

chunks.heading: Why consumer apps are lucrative right now
chunks.text:
Blake gives two reasons.

- **AI:** LLMs let a single builder solve problems that were previously impossible or too expensive. "It would have been virtually impossible to build an AI dating assistant without the use of LLMs."
- **Novel distribution:** TikTok and Instagram are "very solvable right now". Because the platforms are in "bloodbath competition", they have to incentivize new creators and push more views to new accounts than they did a few years ago. That makes influencer, user-generated content, and organic account strategies work for funneling millions of people to a product.

chunks.heading: Finding and validating app ideas
chunks.text:
Blake used a different method for each app.

- **Rizz GPT:** a problem he had observed directly. Friends kept posting in fraternity group chats asking what to say to a girl, so he built an app to answer that.
- **Umax:** found more opportunistically. When people want to become more attractive they spend heavily on skin care, hair care, and gua sha, but no software existed for the problem.
- **Niche signal:** "When you find a niche that's heavily monetized with physical products, that's a good indicator that the niche converts." It is also a sign that software can solve a problem inside it.
- **Validation:** he deep-dives the niche on social media. He creates a fresh account and consumes only that niche's content (for example calorie counting, dieting, and weightlifting for a calorie app). He becomes the target demographic, works out what he wants, and builds that.

Idea areas he thinks are still open:
- A career AI platform for students, rolling fragmented tools (AI LinkedIn image generator, AI resume analysis) into one brand, as a mobile and web app.
- Language learning built on ChatGPT advanced voice mode as a personal tutor. Duolingo makes about $33M a month, roughly $400M a year, and 1% of that market would be a $4M-a-year app.
- An all-in-one AI glow-up app. Umax was a first iteration, and he believes a more valuable one could still make millions.

chunks.heading: The Rizz GPT launch story
chunks.text:
- The first version was bad. It had no notifications, no reviews, a messy design, and a terrible paywall. Early promos produced few downloads and a few dollars.
- He then found two underground, undiscovered creators and paid each $50, $100 total.
- Result: 5 to 10 million views overnight, 45,000 downloads on the first big day, 200,000 downloads that week, and 500,000 that month.
- The app reached about $80k MRR from the start, scaled to a little over $250k MRR, then settled at roughly $150k to $200k MRR.
- Takeaway: an MVP plus a smart marketing strategy is enough to start earning. The app does not need to be perfect.

chunks.heading: Build stack and process
chunks.text:
- **Design:** Figma. He calls learning it one of the biggest unlocks, even for someone who will hire designers off Upwork. His method is to collect reference apps with similar functionality and design, and use them to guide his own.
- **Code:** React Native with Expo, using Cursor as the IDE. Backend is Node.js.
- **Other tools:** CapCut for content, Mercury for startup banking, Upwork for occasional contract work.
- **Hiring on Upwork:** hire five to ten people to do an hour or two of work each, then stick with the best one.

chunks.heading: Marketing: influencers, in-house UGC, and persistence
chunks.text:
Blake uses two main methods.

- **Influencer marketing:** pay someone with an existing audience to promote the product.
- **Internal UGC:** you or a hired creator makes content about the app and posts it on accounts branded around the app. Early on he makes it himself in CapCut, mixing slideshows, faceless video, and talking-to-camera content.
- **Iterate ruthlessly:** try different strategies, and when one produces profitable returns on the time or money invested, "double down and double down and double down."

Most people fail at outreach because they DM ten influencers, get no replies within 24 hours, and give up. Blake's approach is to get creative about reaching them.
- The most profitable Rizz GPT creator was a teenager, 18 or 19, posting for fun, and hard to reach.
- Blake found a Discord link hidden in the creator's Instagram bio, joined it, and sent a message every 10 minutes until the creator replied.
- He also DM'd some creators' mothers asking for a contact to their sons.

chunks.heading: Monetization, margins, and costs
chunks.text:
- **Model:** subscriptions. He says everyone he knows who makes serious money on apps uses them.
- **Pricing:** he generally goes for lower price points. More people can use the app, they tell friends, user sentiment on social media is better, and it is more sustainable for long-term growth. Many apps charge much more.
- **Paywall testing:** he recommends Superwall to split-test offerings (weekly, monthly, yearly), price points, and placements within the app. He says this can take revenue per download from X to 1.5X or 2X.
- **Apple's cut:** 15% officially but closer to 20% in practice on the first $1M of earnings. Beyond that it is 30%, closer to 33% in practice.
- **AI costs:** people overestimate them. Unless an app does image generation or advanced voice mode, backend AI costs are under 3% of revenue. The bulk of expenses are marketing and staff.
