- **Margins by marketing channel:**
  - Internal UGC: about 50% to 80% profit margin.
  - Influencer marketing: about 25% to 70%.
  - Paid ads: about 0% to 30%.
- **Profit figures:** Umax does a little over $100k profit a month consistently (it used to do more). Cal AI does a few hundred thousand dollars of profit a month. He declined to share Rizz GPT's.

chunks.heading: Mindset: urgency and first principles
chunks.text:
- **Urgency:** his most productive periods came when risk and urgency were high. Building Rizz GPT, he was at home making $0 while his parents' house was on the market and friends took six-figure jobs. Building Umax, he had just split from his Rizz GPT team and felt he had something to prove, coding alone on his brother's couch over Thanksgiving. He says to create that sense of urgency if you have "that dog in you."
- **Rizz GPT split:** he left after he and a co-founder kept clashing over who led the company. He told the co-founder that one of them runs it and keeps equity while the other leaves, and the co-founder chose to keep running it.
- **Think from first principles:** step away from what you hear on social media and don't just do what others say. He cites a Naval quote: "If you want to make the wrong decision, ask everybody."
- **Current project:** Apex, an all-in-one self-improvement ecosystem that combines content, a free community, free mobile apps, and low-margin, high-quality physical products. It was about a month and a half old at the time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Day-in-the-life with Blake Anderson, who built Rizz GPT, Umax and other iOS apps to about $10M in sales by 23. He covers his distribution engine (influencer marketing), why he codes in intense sprints, how he thinks about long-term vision, and funding Apex from app cash flow.

chunks.heading: Origin story and the "last shot" mindset
chunks.text:
- Blake grew up outside Philadelphia. As a kid he ran lemonade stands and wrote an ebook, "how to make money as a 7-year-old". He has never had a normal job or internship.
- His father was a successful entrepreneur until Blake was about 12-13, then neurological issues (including secondary progressive MS) sank the businesses. By graduation from Tulane his parents had sold the house and he moved back home. His older brother was lending him money for groceries.
- He started building Riz GPT as he graduated, choosing between a normal job and one last shot on his own. He describes it as a "burn the boats" bet.
- He says he'd "rather live at the extreme with a 50% chance that it all crashes and burns" than live a monotonous life.
- He admits that framing sounds dramatic for "a [__] app called Riz GPT", but says that's how it felt at the time.

chunks.heading: Riz GPT launch and distribution
chunks.text:
- Riz GPT was his first app. He coded it about 12 hours a day for over a month, only coding.
- Launch tactic: find two underrated, unknown TikTok creators and pay each about $50.
- Result: overnight virality, one video at 2 million views and one at 4 million, with hundreds of thousands of downloads.
- Riz GPT hit about $200,000 a month very quickly, and he says he was still walking to and from Starbucks at that point.
- It still makes around $200 a month with little effort.

chunks.heading: Revenue across his apps
chunks.text:
- Blake's tally (iOS plus a small Android amount): about $10 million in total sales.
  - Ci app: $2.4M
  - Improvement Tech / Umax (looksmaxing app): $4.2M
  - Riz GPT, lifetime: $2.6M
- Profit attributable to him is roughly $2.5-3M, after Apple's 30% cut and after giving money to his parents and brother.
- The apps keep earning without him. He estimates that if he stopped working today, the profit attributable to him would still be in the range of $5-10M.
- Riz GPT still does about $200 a month and Umax $50-400 a month (his figures, unclear on timeframe).

chunks.heading: Acquisition channels for the apps
chunks.text:
- Primary channel: influencer marketing.
- Secondary: internal UGC (user generated content) and paid platform ads on Meta and TikTok.
- His view: everything works, but influencers are the most profitable strategy.

chunks.heading: How to learn to code and build fast
chunks.text:
- Blake says coding returns are nonlinear (even "exponential or quadratic"), like surfing or video editing.
- Coding once a day for 50 days beats once a week for 50 weeks, even though both are 50 sessions.
- He recommends long, concentrated stretches. His Riz GPT month was 12 hours a day.
- He codes in Cursor, an AI-powered IDE, and says he is "not very good at coding" himself and leans on AI tools.
- At the time he was building the Apex Improve application.

chunks.heading: Thinking long-term and running a team
chunks.text:
- He doesn't set goals like "make $10 million". He asks how to maximize his impact and the footprint he leaves, and sees money as the resource that funds a long-term vision.
- He works with two close college friends as co-founders. Each owns a primary domain and its processes and stack.
- He wants to pass lessons from earlier ventures to co-founders as fast as possible, with "no ego" and focus on "the information and decisions at hand".
- Team of about five lives and works together in a rented house in San Diego ("the Apex house"), with a daily check-in at a whiteboard.
- He picks surroundings (big views, nature, ocean, hikes) that help him "think clearly".

chunks.heading: Funding Apex from the old apps
chunks.text:
- His next company, Apex, is self-funded from app cash flow.
- The team projects losing about $60-70K a month minimum for the foreseeable future.
- He plans to put at least a few million into making Apex succeed, and says about $1 million is in so far.
- Past app income keeps cash flowing, which lets him fund the bigger vision without outside money.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake walks through three consumer AI utility apps and the playbook behind them: find an untapped social niche, ship a simple app that delivers value, and push it viral with influencer promos. He also covers vetting influencers, making cold outreach unignorable, and why he went big when a copycat appeared.

chunks.heading: Origin story and early hustles
chunks.text:
- As a kid Blake wrote an ebook titled "how to make money as a seven-year-old", and mowed lawns, raked leaves, shoveled driveways and sold candy.
- As a teenager he moved to manipulating game marketplaces: selling Madden Mobile coins, botting RuneScape (he ran the feather market at about 13), selling counterfeit NBA jerseys, building an Ethereum mining machine at 16, and scaling Instagram meme pages.
- His senior-year college marketplace app made no money. He had no job plans, a few thousand dollars invested, and his older brother loaned him money for groceries.
- A roommate asked him what to say to girls on dating apps, a few months after ChatGPT launched. He decided to have ChatGPT generate replies programmatically, with zero software experience and nothing in his bank account.

chunks.heading: RizzGPT: value plus virality
chunks.text:
- The product was simple: upload a screenshot of your messages and get suggested replies.
- He had two co-founders with social media experience. They launched on TikTok and found an untapped niche of "rizz" content, where creators show off how good they are at talking to girls.
- They paid two faceless accounts $50 promos. They got about 200,000 downloads in roughly 5 days and about $80k MRR right away.
- The app was a mess: no notifications, no review prompt, a "horrible" paywall. His takeaway: "the most important thing was we provided value to people and we made it viral and in this space that's really all you need to get started."
- It launched at the start of July and scaled to a bit over $200k MRR over the next few months (he agreed to roughly $2.5M ARR). He parted ways amicably with a co-founder over product direction and kept his equity.
- ChatGPT did about 95% of the code for RizzGPT and about 90% for Umax. He used it as a personal tutor.

chunks.heading: Umax: finding the niche and partnering with an influencer
chunks.text:
- He scanned social media for what was popping and underserved, and landed on "looks maxing": men trying to become more attractive. He argues it cuts through the real motive behind weightlifting.
- He saw two things people wanted: to find out how attractive they are, and how to become more attractive. The GPT Vision API had just come out, so he could send a face photo in and get an analysis back.
- He became obsessed with the content himself first, so he knew which influencers looks maxers would actually listen to.
- He brought on Sam Zia, a top looks-maxing influencer, plus his older brother for engineering. For a partner he looks for someone "hardworking, intelligent and a true entrepreneur", not just a creator.
- The launch started with one Sam video that got about 100,000 views and a few thousand downloads. The first month brought about $100,000 in revenue.
- He got Sam through an intro. Lucas Pactor connected them after Blake messaged him about the app.

chunks.heading: The copycat and going big early
chunks.text:
- In mid-January a copycat copied the marketing, the outputs and the scoring metrics, and passed Umax in the App Store.
- Blake had been holding off on scaling to improve retention first. His rule is not to "burn through the entire Forest before we had optimized the app for retention for LTV."
- The copycat didn't care about user experience, so he decided it was better to burn through the forest and pursue the long-term vision later than to be beaten in the short term.
- In 3-4 days he put over $200,000 into influencer partnerships, more than all the revenue the app had made up to then. He calls it a massive gamble.
- Umax went to over $500,000 MRR. The copycat hit in two weeks the downloads that took Umax a month and a half, but Blake says Umax then had about 4x their downloads and 4x their revenue.
- He chose not to add features that might pull focus from the core loop: download, scan your face, get results.

chunks.heading: How he approaches influencer marketing
chunks.text:
- Most influencers produce negative ROI, but some produce 10x ROI. Running as many of those as possible is highly scalable.
- Paid platform ads let you split test 100 creatives and double down. Influencer attribution is hard, so you need a "Spidey-like sense" of who converts.
- He looks at what an influencer's comment section says about the strength of their community and whether it follows their recommendations.
- Companies fail by sending 100 DMs, taking every yes, or going through an agency.
- For one-off promos you have to know the space deeply. For a deep partnership, pick someone who is also a builder.
- Cal AI uses paid influencer marketing with no partner. It competes against big incumbents in a huge category, and no single influencer could out-return what the team can do in-house. A partner makes more sense in a smaller niche like looks maxing, where the top person carries the market.

chunks.heading: Outreach: be unignorable, lead with value
chunks.text:
- Don't send one DM and give up. Try TikTok, then Instagram, then Discord, and even their mom: "you have to make yourself unignorable."
- The same message on four platforms makes a response far more likely than on one. It takes about 2 minutes. He says there is a spammy way and a good way: lead with real insight.
- Quality beats quantity. The best cold messages give something thoughtful before asking for anything, rather than "can you give me advice on X."
- Zach slid into his DMs at 16 with a specific insight ("you're doing X, you should be doing Y"). After a few calls Blake was working with him as an equal partner.

chunks.heading: Cal AI and the playbook model
chunks.text:
- He met two 17-year-olds around March or April. They saw calorie tracking as one of the biggest App Store categories, but a static one, so the thesis was to apply new AI to make tracking more accurate and easier.
- It launched a bit over a month before this recording and had done about $100,000 in revenue in that time.
- Zach Yadegari is CEO and Henry Langmack is CTO. Blake provides high-level advice and the playbooks that made RizzGPT and Umax work, without a multi-year time commitment.
- He says the strategy is "100% replicable" and invites skilled, hard-working people with good ideas to DM him.

chunks.heading: Finding ideas and what not to take as advice
chunks.text:
- New AI capabilities have expanded what can be built, and building is cheaper than ever. He built his first two apps with ChatGPT.
- If you think and say what everyone else does, you reach the same conclusions. To find novel ideas, orient your life differently and read between the lines.
- He avoids crowded categories like AI CRMs and email agents, which he sees as bloodbaths. He cites Peter Thiel: "competition is for losers."
- Early wins are a way to fund bigger plays later, such as a broader male self-improvement vision.
- He doesn't think advice transfers. What worked for him may not work for others, and people urging the safe path mean well but don't know you like you do.
- He rejects the idea that you must work 16 hours a day, and wants time for the gym, friends and being outdoors.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson, co-founder of Cal AI (now over $2.5M a month), reflects on a year of wins and failed projects (Apex, the first 10X). He argues one-feature AI apps are saturated, that viral distribution is now a volume game on warmed-up accounts, and that the real bottleneck for builders is personal skill.

chunks.heading: Why technical skill matters more in the AI era
chunks.text:
- Blake rejects the idea that learning technical skills is pointless because AI will write the code. He says "there has never been a more high leveraged time to become technical in human history."
- The form changes: less scanning Stack Overflow to debug, more using AI to code and build. He compares it to abstraction layers (machine code, then interpreted languages, now largely human language), but the underlying engineering knowledge is still needed.
- Common trait of successful founders he sees: they apply AI to everything they do.
- Example: he ran a two-hour paid trial for a 10X designer on Upwork with 5 to 10 candidates. One produced far more and better work, including custom icons and a design system, because he knew which AI tools generate clean mobile app icons.
- Other examples: content creators using ChatGPT for hooks and scripts, engineers for code, designers for icon libraries.
- He sees the gap between people who can apply these tools and those who can't as a large market inefficiency.

chunks.heading: Where the AI app opportunity has moved
chunks.text:
- Blake's contrarian take: more mobile apps hit $1M+ ARR in 2024 than will in 2025 on "one or two key AI functions," because GPT Vision let builders upgrade old app categories and that innovation has largely been done.
- His examples of the earlier wave: Cali's photo-to-calorie logging was a function that was previously unsolved.
- He expects more apps overall, but not the super simple one- or two-function ones. He sees too much copycatting of already-popular experiences.
- His advice: stop over-indexing on one viral feature. Chain multiple prompts and user steps into fully AI-native experiences, because "the level of complexity necessary to succeed will continue to increase as will the size of the outcomes."
- Because new capabilities arrive faster than products get built on them, he says there is more alpha in being close to the ground and knowing which tools and resources emerge first.

chunks.heading: How he's building 10X (version 2.0)
chunks.text:
- 10X's long-term vision is to redefine personalized education.
- The first version was a Duolingo-style "learn anything" app. He built it in about two weeks and launched with 2 to 3 days of marketing. It hit $10K MRR, but RPM to CPM didn't make sense. He knew how long and how much capital it would take to reach $1M ARR, so he paused it and went back to ideation.
- He built it during PMF or Die, a challenge to hit $1M ARR in under 90 days. He left after 36 days locked in a New York apartment on a 24/7 livestream. He says the mental toll hurt his ability to think clearly, and he doesn't think it is a conducive way to build a business.
- He and his co-founder on that product parted ways ("not the right fit"). He also names a flawed UX design as a cause of the failure.
- The new innovation angle is customized, auto-updating content:
  - A long onboarding flow that captures what the user wants to learn.
  - A generated assessment during onboarding to gauge knowledge by topic.
  - A feed auto-populated from those results, updating as the user learns.
- His pattern across products: pick one thing to innovate on per app and keep the rest standard. For Cali it was photo calorie logging.

chunks.heading: Distribution thesis: UGC is saturating, account volume is the next lever
chunks.text:
- Almost two years ago he tweeted that UGC demand would rise exponentially as AI lets more small teams build apps. He now says everyone knows this and "there is relatively very little alpha left" in it, though he still believes in AI-generated UGC.
- His view of the bottleneck: creating thousands of pieces of AI UGC is no longer the edge. Getting them posted on warmed-up accounts is.
- His example system: 100 warmed-up accounts, 3 videos per account per day, so 300 videos a day. At a conservative 500 views each, that is 150,000 views per day as a floor, before counting videos that hit millions.
- Reasoning: social algorithms follow a power law, so one viral video produces outsized profit for the creator, the UGC creator or the brand. More shots on goal means a higher chance one lands.
- He cites Temu's affiliate system, with a huge volume of content going out daily, as the best example of this volume approach.
- He believes this volume-and-warmed-accounts play is a major opportunity in viral content, and says he is thinking about it deeply for 10X.

chunks.heading: Killing projects fast and keeping failures public
chunks.text:
- Scorecard he gave: UMAX was just over $5M ARR a year earlier and is now over $3M. RizzGPT was just over $2M and is now about $1.5M. Both dipped because he put little time into them.
- Cali went from $100K MRR to over $2.5M a month, which he says is over $30M annualized.
- He spent early time scaling Cali, then moved to Apex, an all-in-one self-improvement ecosystem built on free apps, with content and CPG (supplements) as the long-term play. He had two co-founders on it.
- He decided Apex had a flawed macro thesis and wasn't the right project. He also wanted to be building AI technology.
- He defends moving on quickly as closing the feedback loop: "I'm not going to allow my feedback loops to lengthen... when I know what the end answer is going to be." If the loop says no, he kills it and moves on.
- He admits he got too confident and cocky, assuming he could copy and paste earlier formulas onto bigger ideas. He now wants bigger-impact products, which he says don't come from one-function apps.
- He says he failed for years before earning a full-time income, then did it back to back to back. He now aims to build a legacy and says years of repeated failure won't make him quit.

chunks.heading: Cali's co-founder structure
chunks.text:
- Blake describes his role arc at Cali: early on he was "the coach." He put in most of the capital, handled UX, and brought his marketing strategy and influencer relationships from previous projects.
- Over time Zach became the CEO and the one running the company. Blake now acts as a resource, covering cash flow and the Apple payout timing and helping with high-level strategy, while the team runs daily operations.
- Roles he describes:
  - Zach: CEO, leads from the front and is the public face. Blake calls him exceptionally mature and hardworking, a 17-year-old CEO of a $30M ARR business.
  - Henry: CTO, engineers the product and accepts that he doesn't need to represent the company.
  - Jake: head of growth, leads influencer campaigns and the internal growth team.
- Why it works, in his view: no one needs the spotlight, and everyone knows they can claim the credit when they eventually step back, with full support from the others.

chunks.heading: Learning, college, advice and skill over followers
chunks.text:
- On college: he dropped out after a year and a half, still thinks going was a good decision, and thinks he left at the right time. He argues that for an intelligent, hardworking person, self-learning something you care about is faster than school.
- Zach example: a ~34 ACT, president of his robotics club, rejected from about 20 schools, accepted to UT Austin, U Miami and Georgia Tech, and now runs a $30M ARR business.
- Two learning priorities for 2025 and the next five-plus years:
  1. Become proficient with AI tools in your own industry (chatbots, image generation, industry-specific tools) and start creating immediately.
  2. Keep building time-tested foundational knowledge (calculus, statistics, psychology, philosophy). AI tool skill alone won't carry a career; you need a developed worldview to know which questions to ask.
- He cites Ed Thorp, who studied physics and math, rejected the consensus that roulette was unpredictable, and built a device to predict where the ball lands.
- He says people will tell you what you can't do with AI, such as building a full app with ChatGPT, which he did, and still don't believe him.
- On advice: people rarely give it hoping for the worst, but consider the source. He cites Peter Thiel as someone who rarely gives advice because what worked for one person doesn't transfer.
- His closing lesson: reject what he says too, learn foundational knowledge, build your skills, and "follow your gut." If it fails, you at least did it your way and learned the lesson.
- He deleted Twitter, Instagram and TikTok because of the "skill to follower ratio": he doesn't want followers to outpace his actual skill.
- His current routine: coding every day, reading textbooks on agentic and complex systems, and studying multivariable calculus with Math Academy.
- His view of the bottleneck: for builders it is skill, not capital or hiring, because "most of the best talent is unhirable."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake explains how he built two consumer AI apps with almost no coding background, using ChatGPT as tutor and code writer. He covers shipping fast, ruthless marketing iteration, betting all revenue on influencers when a copycat appeared, and spotting niches outside the Silicon Valley echo chamber.

chunks.heading: How Blake built Riz GPT (now Plug AI) with ChatGPT and found its first growth channel
chunks.text:
- Riz GPT is an AI dating assistant that launched in July 2023 and is now named Plug AI. It reached $2.5M ARR.
- The idea came from a college roommate who kept asking what to say to girls on dating apps. Blake pasted a transcript into ChatGPT, found the answer too "AI-like", and decided to fix it through prompt engineering.
- He had zero software experience, only a little Python. He says "ChatGPT taught me how to build the app and then ChatGPT provided the main functionality for the app". About 99% of the code was written by ChatGPT.
- The app was simple: a gradient background, a logo and two buttons. You upload a screenshot and get responses.
- An incumbent Riz app existed but had not gone mainstream or viral.
- At launch, marketing was not sticking. Blake found an untapped niche on TikTok and paid $50 for each of two promos, $100 total.
- Result: over 200,000 downloads in six days and $80,000 MRR right away. It scaled to a little over $200,000 MRR within a couple of months.
- The app launched without notifications and without review requests. He backfilled those afterward.

chunks.heading: Launch early on single-function consumer utility apps
chunks.text:
- Blake's lesson from Riz GPT: "you can learn that [stuff] along the way, the most important thing is just get your product out there."
- He applies this to consumer utility apps with a few functions. It does not apply to social networks.
- The reasoning: ship, get the insights, find out whether it works, then backfill what you need.
- He says there is "no reason to delay the launch" for a few-function tool.

chunks.heading: Marketing consumer apps: a ruthless cycle of iteration
chunks.text:
- Blake rejects one-size-fits-all advice such as "you need to use this TikTok strategy" or YouTube Shorts, Reels, Reddit or X. Certain channels may work better at certain times.
- He calls the most important factor for buzz and virality "a ruthless cycle of iteration", meaning constant testing of new strategies.
- Time to find the winning formula:
  - Riz GPT: a couple of weeks.
  - UMAX: about a month and a half.
  - Cal AI: more than a month and still not found at the time, though it was already near $100K MRR.
- Finding the first channel is not the end. Crossing the first threshold of views "doesn't mean that you figured out your final form". He says to keep iterating on marketing until you are finished with the company.

chunks.heading: Building an app with ChatGPT: his process
chunks.text:
- Building Riz GPT took him about a month. He says it would have been quicker had he known the IDEs.
- UMAX was built in about a month. For UMAX, roughly 85% of the code was still written by ChatGPT.
- Steps for a consumer mobile app:
  1. Start with the designs. Decide what the product looks like.
  2. Pick the stack: React Native, SwiftUI or Kotlin. He builds in SwiftUI.
  3. Describe the design and the button functionality very clearly to ChatGPT. You can also upload a screenshot of the design.
  4. Ask ChatGPT to write the code, paste it into Xcode and preview it.
  5. If the spacing is off, adjust it yourself or ask ChatGPT to adjust it.
- Takeaway: "it's a lot easier than you think, you just have to start." Early growing pains (learning the IDE, code that won't compile) pass quickly. He describes ChatGPT as having your own professional tutor at your fingertips.

chunks.heading: UMAX: finding the idea and building it fast
chunks.text:
- UMAX is a looksmaxing app. You scan your face, get a rating, and receive personalized recommendations to become more attractive. It launched at the start of December 2023, two days after Thanksgiving, and reached a little over $6M ARR.
- Blake left Riz GPT in mid-to-late October 2023 after a disagreement with a co-founder over product direction. They split amicably and he kept his equity. He was effectively unemployed, hopping between friends' couches and his brother's couch.
- Idea finding: he saw looksmaxing growing and judged it the next step after lifting content, since most men lift to appeal to women. He became "a student of the game" by engaging with all the content and thinking like someone interested in looksmaxing.
- Two unmet needs he spotted:
  - People wanted to know how attractive they were. Whole subreddits and "rate me" comments existed for this.
  - People wanted personalized tips, but the tips online were generic.
- The GPT Vision API was coming out, so he could prompt engineer face analysis instead of training an ML model. Early tests recommended shaving a patchy beard and skincare for forehead acne.
- He coded round two with ChatGPT and launched in about a month and a few days. December revenue was about $100,000. By the first half of January the app was around $200K MRR.
- His brother came up with the Madden-style rating system, which Blake calls the most pivotal decision for the company's trajectory.

chunks.heading: Responding to a copycat by deploying all revenue into influencers
chunks.text:
- In January, a competitor copied UMAX completely: the app and the marketing strategy.
- Blake's original plan was to grow slowly and improve LTV and the offering before "burning the forest" through core users. He had done a couple hundred thousand downloads.
- As a bootstrapped company, he faced a choice: go slow and risk being overtaken, or fight back. Fighting meant trading some long-term conversion, since pushing millions of downloads before the product is in final form makes users hard to reconvert. Given the market, he decided to fight back.
- Within three days he deployed over $200,000 on influencer campaigns, which was all the revenue and earnings to that point.
- Results over about five days:
  - MRR went from $200K to over $500K.
  - About 100,000 downloads in one day.
  - Daily revenue of about $50K, $40K, $15K and $25K.
- He did not sleep much during this period. He was on the phone with influencers, coding, and working with engineers and his social media manager. Afterward the app plateaued at a little over $500K MRR.

chunks.heading: Reinvesting profits, no plan B, and team and co-founder choices
chunks.text:
- Blake says he is very risk-taking and has no Plan B: "either this works or it goes bad and if it goes bad we'll assess that then."
- His pattern is doubling down: Riz GPT money funded UMAX, and UMAX money will fund his next big play.
- On co-founders, he has no formula. He chooses based on the role and the gaps in his own skill set.
  - Riz GPT: two co-founders from his college marketplace app.
  - UMAX: a near solo start, then his older brother and an influencer as co-founders.
  - Cal AI: two 17-year-old co-founders, Zach Yadegari and Henry Langmack, with equal ownership.
- On solo versus team, he cites the "85% of a watermelon is better than 100% of a grape" idea. If two people each make 80% of decisions right with no overlap, combined they make 96% right.
- On motivating a team, he says he does not have it fully solved. His approach is to play to who you are and not imitate someone else. He admits he can be hard, difficult and stubborn, but he really cares, and that shows.

chunks.heading: Cal AI and where he sees opportunity in AI
chunks.text:
- Cal AI is an AI calorie tracker. The thesis: calorie trackers take too much time and he quit every one he used after a couple of days. With Cal AI you take a picture and get the calorie analysis.
- It also keeps the standard features: barcode scanning and manual macro input. Photo capture is the differentiator.
- It was around $100K MRR at the time, in a space with about 50 big competitors. He was comfortable sharing it early because a copycat would have to beat all those incumbents too. UMAX remained his main priority.
- Opportunity areas he points to with GPT-4o and native multimodal voice:
  - Audio and social simulation, including dating simulation, to counter people becoming more antisocial as typing becomes the main way to socialize.
  - Learning apps, such as a language tutor or a voice quiz tool that tests what you know and recommends resources.
- Package and reskin: even if ChatGPT can do something natively, "the vast majority of people" won't know they can use it there. So there is still a large opportunity in packaging or reskinning an LLM capability.
- Advice to builders: deviate from the norm in what you think, say and do. He warns that the Silicon Valley bubble is an echo chamber where too many people work on the same talked-about ideas. He says "a lot of the alpha lies when you push past the veil of the public domain". Nobody was talking about an AI looksmaxing app when he built it.
- He says video games, such as strategy and life simulations, give rapid repetitions of economic and strategic tradeoffs without putting real capital, time or stakes on the line.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson explains how he went from serial teenage side hustles to Rizz GPT (200K downloads, 80K MRR in a week) and UMAX (about $700K in its best month) by spotting a popping TikTok niche, using new AI tech, and buying influencer promos. He covers RPM vs CPM math for influencer deals, why apps are underserved, and why he is shifting to a mission-driven venture.

chunks.heading: From a dating-app "wingman" to Rizz GPT: how the first product launched
chunks.text:
- In June 2023 Blake moved back home after graduating from Tulane. He worked from his attic and a coffee shop, with no income and no plan B.
- The idea came from a college roommate who kept asking what to say to girls on dating apps. ChatGPT had launched a few months earlier, and Blake believed it could generate those replies programmatically.
- The product, Rizz GPT, lets a user upload a screenshot of a conversation and get suggested replies.
- His co-founders had social media marketing experience but none with consumer apps.
- Launch results: instant product-market fit and virality. $50 promos with underground "rizz" accounts on TikTok drove 200,000 downloads and $80K MRR within a week.
- He later scaled the app to a little over $200,000 MRR, then split amicably from his co-founders over product direction and kept his equity.
- Tools and skills: he double-majored in finance and CS, but says Tulane's CS program was weak. ChatGPT acted as his tutor and wrote most of the early code, in SwiftUI.
- The launch version lacked basics like notifications, reviews and a formal back end (no user table). He caught up by asking people who had built successful apps what to do after finding product-market fit.
- He argues going full-time beats a side hustle. He says people who plan to take a job and pursue entrepreneurship later find their expenses scale and quitting becomes impossible.

chunks.heading: The repeatable playbook behind Rizz GPT and UMAX
chunks.text:
Blake describes one strategy used for both apps:
1. Identify a popping niche on TikTok.
2. Build a product that solves a consumer need in that niche.
3. Scale through creator promos.

- UMAX came after the split, while he was hopping between friends' couches. He saw the looksmaxing trend and brought in Sam as a co-founder and his older brother.
- The need it serves: guys want to know how attractive they are and how to become more attractive (hair, skincare, etc.).
- After the first few promos, he says it became "a game of scaling from there."
- The best month so far was February, at about $700,000 in revenue.
- Across all his apps he is at roughly $1 million a month in revenue.
- He describes a two-part timing edge:
  - Market timing: Google Trends for looksmaxing was steadily rising.
  - Technology timing: the GPT Vision API had just been released. It let him build a face-analysis app without custom-training an ML vision model, which he says could cost tens to a hundred thousand dollars.
- His framework for ideas: ask what new technology was just enabled, and what popular space it can be applied to. Where both meet there is little competition.
- He calls UMAX an "opportunistic play" for a trend and not a guaranteed 30-year market. He says "ready, fire, aim" suits that kind of play.
- He says to take your time if you are building an empire where public perception matters from the start.

chunks.heading: Fighting a copycat competitor with a $200K influencer blitz
chunks.text:
- A competitor copied UMAX's outputs and ratings feature almost exactly. They reached in about 2 weeks the downloads UMAX took a little over a month to reach, and pumped influencers from the start.
- Blake had wanted to go slower and improve the offering, including a course-like section on skincare and self-improvement. The competitor cared only about the ratings, which he says are the most viral component.
- His decision: either let them become the top name and try to overtake them later, or go big immediately. He chose to go big.
- Over about 3 days he deployed a little over $200,000 on influencers, which was all the money the company had made to that point.
- Tactics:
  - He made a list of the biggest influencers in the niche and DMed them.
  - He asked for exclusive contracts, so they could not work with the competitor.
  - One example: a $50,000 wire for a month, for a set number of posts, with approval rights and no view clauses (very favorable to the creator).

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing math: RPM vs CPM
chunks.text:
- A promo is profitable if its RPM (revenue per thousand views) after variable costs exceeds its CPM (cost per thousand views).
- Step one is to find the average RPM within a niche. Example: if an influencer's 1 million views produce $5,000 in sales, the RPM is $5.
- With a $5 RPM, he would target influencers at about a $3 CPM, paying $3,000 per million views.
- Variable costs differ by business. For physical goods they are the cost of goods, shipping and Stripe fees. For his apps the main one is Apple's cut.
- Apple takes 15% up to $1 million in sales and 30% after that.
- He says Android users notoriously don't convert, so Apple's marketplace is where paying users are.
- Apple also gives free distribution once an app does well. About half of UMAX's downloads now come from Apple pushing it out, driven by past downloads and positive reviews.
- Hit rate: DM about 100 influencers, about 10 respond, and perhaps 3 produce profitable ads. Most people fail because they can't identify those 3.
- Knowing your market and being your own customer helps you judge which influencers and messaging will convert.
- Lessons from his teenage ventures:
  - From selling counterfeit NBA jerseys he learned to negotiate promos with Instagram meme pages.
  - Those deals paid a set amount as long as the post hit at least Y views, with an incentive if it exceeded Z.
- Paid ads: Rizz GPT and UMAX used little paid advertising because they are inherently viral. A promo post tends to outperform the creator's average, since people comment "no way bro is using AI to analyze his face." For Cal AI, his most recent app, he has started paid ads and is still assessing ROAS.

chunks.heading: Why apps: the gap between developers and social-media marketers
chunks.text:
- Blake sees an opportunity in the overlap between two groups. Software developers don't understand social media virality, and "internet money" kids don't understand software development. Few people sit in the middle.
- His argument: in a niche where physical products earn around a $2 RPM, a competent app can earn about a $5 RPM. The people viewing that content have usually never seen an app for the space.
- With that higher RPM, you can pump money into creator promos faster than competitors who sell physical products. This works especially well if you also know how to generate views.
- He adds that consumer apps are largely a game of maximizing revenue per user and getting as many users as possible.
- Some developers he knows make millions a month and say they don't care what they build.
- He says he doesn't plan to stay in the consumer app space, because it isn't mission-driven and he doesn't find it deeply fulfilling.

chunks.heading: Iteration, doubling down and when to quit
chunks.text:
- Blake's teenage ventures:
  - Raking leaves and shoveling driveways.
  - Selling candy.
  - Selling Madden Mobile coins.
  - Botting RuneScape.
  - Building an Ethereum mining machine.
  - Running Instagram meme page promos.
- Each made roughly $50 to a couple thousand dollars.
- His lesson: iteration is valuable because you learn fast, but eventually you must double down on your skills. He did lots of learning and little doubling down as a teenager.
- That wide skill set paid off when Rizz GPT took off.
- On the college marketplace app he was building before Rizz GPT, Harry Gestetner (founder of FanFix, who built a college marketplace app before FanFix) told him, kindly, that he wouldn't continue it. Blake says "sometimes you got to call it quits" is advice that is not prominent enough online.
- He says failure is acceptable if you learn. It is better to have failed and learned than to have failed without learning or never tried.
- He says the biggest driver of entrepreneurial success is not intelligence or hard work but risk tolerance and willingness to sacrifice.
- On his own edge: he says his superpower is thinking differently from most people. He credits creative logical insight and spotting new opportunities for Rizz GPT and UMAX, and says he is not the hardest worker or the most intelligent.
- His grind in 2023: after graduating he worked only on Rizz GPT, from a Starbucks from about 6am to 6pm, then continued at home. He says it didn't feel like a sacrifice at the time. After that period, he says, you can spend your time more freely, and he now works less than his 9-to-5 friends.

chunks.heading: Reinvesting profits and the Apex plan
chunks.text:
- Blake's thinking on capital: he views money as a tool and leverage. He cites Walter Isaacson, his former professor and the biographer of Elon Musk and Steve Jobs, on mission-orientedness and risk tolerance. His example is Elon repeatedly pouring winnings into the next venture (Zip2 into PayPal, PayPal into SpaceX and Tesla).
- He quotes Peter Thiel's takeaway that maybe "the rest of us don't take enough" risk.
- He argues the highest-return investment is combining capital with his own skill set, rather than the S&P 500 or real estate.
- He says to work on things where, even if you fail, you come out ahead. In drop shipping or trading, failure leaves you with essentially nothing. A hard mission-driven pursuit leaves you with skills and knowledge even if it fails.
- Apex is his next company: an all-in-one male self-improvement ecosystem. It will include free apps (workouts, meditation, nutrition and others) and social media content from a creator house.
- The mission is to reorient how self-improvement and entrepreneurship are framed online, away from "get jacked to get girls" and "get money for materialistic things."
- Funding:
  - $500,000 from HF0, the San Francisco accelerator, for a few percent equity plus a SAFE note.
  - At least $500,000 of his own money from UMAX profits, probably more.
  - Spending on development, the house, food and flying influencers in to film.
  - Some profits go to his parents. UMAX and Rizz GPT earnings are being set aside to fund Apex.
- On HF0: it is a house of about 20 people and roughly 10 startups. He says it taught him what it means to be truly mission-oriented.
- His 10-year goal is to influence society positively by redefining self-improvement and entrepreneurship for young people.
- On co-founders: he says to pick people with moral integrity above all, and says it matters most when partners part ways. He notes the right choice depends on the time horizon and structure.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson explains how he went from kid entrepreneur to launching Rizz GPT, UMax and Cali by packaging new AI tech around core human insecurities and desires. He covers influencer sourcing (take many shots, judge creators by comment sections), content briefs, pricing by channel, co-founder equity, and where he sees opportunity now (AI content, app-to-web, AI hardware).

chunks.heading: How Blake Found and Validated AI App Ideas
chunks.text:
- Blake launched Rizz GPT, an AI app for dating-app replies, in July 2023, a few months after ChatGPT came out.
- The idea started when a roommate asked what to text a girl.
- Blake typed the transcript into ChatGPT by hand and the answer was decent.
- He then tried prompt engineering and decided it was a viable product.
- The product let users screenshot a dating-app chat and paste it into the app for a response.
- The app went from zero to $83,000 in MRR within about three days of launch.
- He had tried many ventures before: an ebook at age nine, a lawnmowing business, candy sales in school, dropshipping, Instagram meme pages, an Ethereum mining machine, and a college marketplace app. Individual ventures earned from hundreds of dollars up to about $20,000, but nothing sustainable.
- He says his products benefit from being first to market and from targeting "core human insecurities or desires". He does not start with an over-intellectualized use case and then ask how to make it viral, which he finds much harder.
- Rizz GPT drew on people's wish to get dates. UMax, where you photograph your face and the AI rates your attractiveness and how to improve it, drew on appearance insecurity.
- On timing, he built the whole UMax product beforehand so that when OpenAI's GPT Vision became production-ready he could plug in the endpoint and submit to the App Store. He launched about two days after it hit production-level rate limits.
- He had seen the looksmaxing niche growing and had several market theses at the time. He calls it luck but says he was deliberately analyzing the factors.
- UMax made $100,000 in its first month, $200,000 in the second and $700,000 in the third.
- The looksmaxing community was tight-knit, large and not yet monetized, so he got "immediate product market fit".
- He worked with roughly 8 to 12 creators with large followings to reach the first $100,000.
- He believes more single-function viral AI apps reaching millions in annual revenue were built in 2024 than will be built in 2025. The obvious use cases are taken: AI to talk to girls, rate your face and track calories (the three he built).
- Opportunity remains, with Cluely as an example. Cluely is a hidden laptop tool for cheating on interviews, built by his friend Roy Lee. It is more complex than his own apps and still very viral.
- "The alpha is becoming harder to capture."
- In a period of rapid AI progress, he says the most important skill is picking the right things to work on.
- He thinks it would be a bad idea to wear "complete blinders" on one project for years if it ignores new AI developments. He moves on quickly to stay at the frontier.

chunks.heading: Influencer and Organic Marketing: Volume, Comment Sections and Briefs
chunks.text:
- His influencer approach is high volume. He says to DM hundreds of influencers per day and not fixate on a few dream names. "If you're not DMing hundreds of influencers per day... you're not taking enough shots."
- He pays flat fees with minimum-view clauses. His example is $10,000 with the expectation of at least 2 million views.
- Costs vary by niche. A target CPM might be $5 per 1,000 views, but some creators quote $20 per 1,000.
- Edtech is expensive. Fintech and finance creators are the most expensive, with CPMs of $50 or more.
- He also examines view quality, not just view count.
- If an app isn't inherently viral, he says influencer and organic marketing is "an uphill battle", because it relies on organic recommendation engines.
- Organic is harder to track than platform ads. His team uses automated spreadsheets with video links, views, likes and engagement over time, mapped to downloads.
- Beginners don't need that. Compare each video's views over time against downloads and conversions, and build intuition for which hooks and creators convert.
- He says strong organic marketing "comes down to a deep understanding of statistics and psychology". Psychology covers hooks, messaging and negotiating with creators. Statistics covers inferring what converts, then leaning into those creators and hooks.
- His main creator-selection rule is engaged comment sections. Follower count mattered in the 2010s, then views, and now content quality.
- A video can get hundreds of thousands of views in 6 seconds and still not convert.
- An engaged comment section implies either a deeply trusting fanbase or content engaging enough that people leave thoughtful replies.
- He wants comments with insights or applause, not a stream of fire emojis. Top comments should have good like counts, and there should be sub-reply conversations. A "community" should exist in the comments.
- This is not a perfect one-to-one mapping, but he calls it a very underrated metric. People unwilling to engage in comments are unlikely to click through to the product.
- The team computes median views, average likes and average comments with basic functions, but evaluation is mostly intuitive.
- He uses a content brief PDF for every creator. It includes ways to integrate the product, example videos that did well, and basic rules such as showing the product for at least two seconds and before the 15-second mark, and tagging the app.
- Creators send videos for approval before posting. He may drop that step as he comes to trust certain creators.
- The brief "saves both parties time" and signals professionalism.

chunks.heading: Pricing and Distribution Fit
chunks.text:
- He reverse-engineers distribution when evaluating ideas. It helps to know the distribution strategy before building.
- Engineers tend to think only about technical feasibility. Growth people tend to think only about whether the channel exists and whether customers can be acquired for less than they earn.
- He advises understanding both marketing and engineering well enough to see the playing field, without being extremely technical or a deep TikTok expert.
- Distribution informs pricing. Paid ads suit a high-LTV product with a higher price point, such as $20 per month, or a free trial then $100 per year.
- Organic is more conducive to lower price points, such as $30 per year or $4 per week. He says he has used these pricing strategies.
- Product and distribution form a positive feedback loop.
- His shorthand is to study Silicon Valley for product and dropshipping for marketing. Dropshipping has minimal product differentiation and competes on generating cheap views. Silicon Valley emphasizes product over distribution.
- He thinks there is a lot of value at the intersection of the two.

chunks.heading: Opportunity Ideas: App-to-Web, Services and AI Content
chunks.text:
- He calls helping apps optimize app-to-web payments one of the greatest current opportunities. A recent US court ruling lets mobile apps offer web payments.
- Apple takes 30% of revenue for apps earning over $1 million a year, and 15% under that.
- He and others he knows have started testing it. He expects at least a 20% increase in proceeds for apps above the $1 million mark, and also over 20% for smaller apps. He says the real figure is "well over 20%" but won't give it.
- His team has about 10 different strategies to test, and he calls it an unsolved problem space.
- He suggests an agency that offers to do it free for a reference client, then uses that name to win paying clients on a performance basis. He thinks such an agency could scale past $50,000 a month in profit.
- For zero to $10,000 a month, he says the most important skill is becoming very skilled with AI tools.
- As an example, a designer he hired on Upwork produced far more in a 2-hour paid design challenge than nine others by using an AI tool to generate icons.
- He would apply AI skill to content creation: generating AI content and distributing it across platforms. Generating a few million views a month for a company could earn $10,000 or more a month. He says few people do AI content really well.
- Another option he gives is a UGC agency working with app founders.
- He cites the "sell shovels in a gold rush" idea. Building AI apps has a lower probability of success than servicing the people building them.
- Even so, more people overall will make a lot of money from AI apps than from servicing them.
- Servicing is generally easier, less grindy and has more upside if it works. His examples of big service-side companies are Cursor and Lovable.
- He personally enjoys building consumer products, and he advises doing things you find interesting and enjoyable because that is where you will put in the most hours and creativity.

chunks.heading: Co-founders, Equity and Expectations
chunks.text:
- He is a big advocate of co-founders. His apps have all been built with partners.
- Rizz GPT had three founders: Blake did the engineering, Alex the design and Evan the marketing. Together they reached $250,000 a month within three months.
- He and one co-founder disagreed about the product's direction. They concluded one of them had to leave, and he left but kept his equity. They have since reconnected.
- For UMax he brought in his older brother, who did data analytics work and helped with backend engineering, and Sam Zia, an influencer in the looksmaxing niche. Both were half-partners and part-time until the third month, when they went full-time.
- Cali has four co-founders. Zach and Henry approached him after seeing his success. Zach gave him a list of ideas and Blake chose the AI calorie tracker.
- Blake acted as coach, supplying marketing strategy and capital. Henry and Zach ran the day to day. Jake Castillo joined as the fourth co-founder and CMO after it started succeeding.
- Zach, Henry and Blake split equity three ways equally at the start.
- He says Cali is on track for over $30 million in revenue in 2025.
- His reasoning: equal splits keep everyone incentivized, and unequal splits could have led people to leave after it succeeded.
- His line is "it's a lot better to have 50% of a watermelon than 100% of a grape". The question isn't your share of the upside but whether you can capture it at all.
- Alone, he thinks Rizz GPT might have made $10,000 to $20,000 a month, or never launched.
- Co-founders can go badly, and he has experienced that.
- He says the biggest issues come from unclear expectations. Examples are one founder wanting a billion-dollar business while another wants $50,000 a month, or someone failing to deliver engineering. Define responsibilities clearly from the start.
- Good co-founders are usually found organically through relationships, not by searching urgently.

chunks.heading: Choosing Projects, Persistence and Taking Advice
chunks.text:
- He has worked full-time on five projects in two years: Rizz GPT, UMax, Cali, Apex and 10X. He still does some work on UMax, a good amount on Cali, and has moved on from Apex and 10X.
- On when to quit, he says many people work on the wrong projects for too long, while others don't give a project time to mature. The right call depends on the person and the product.
- He tries to ask whether it's really time to move on or he just wants new excitement.
- He thinks building 20 products a year is probably too fast.
- A universal principle for him is to optimize for learning. Even if a project fails, he wants to come out with transferable skills. He says day trading fails this test, because failing at it teaches little transferable knowledge.
- The counter-example is Speechify, which took years before succeeding. He says Sensor Tower implies at least $50 million a year in revenue, and the real number is higher. He therefore avoids bold claims where there are many counterfactuals.
- He warns against mimetic desire, doing a thing because many others are doing it. This tends to give the same results as everyone else. He prefers reading between the lines and seeing opportunity others miss.
- He chose AI apps over TikTok Shop despite friends succeeding there, because he wanted learning and AI's upward trajectory.
- He currently explores AI hardware with his brother, aiming at local inference: an open-source LLM on a small processor with no cloud connection.
- Their first build is an AI pocket recorder using an ESP32 board, a microphone, an SD card, Bluetooth and a lithium-ion battery. Audio is uploaded to a computer, transcribed and summarized.
- He cites Plaud as proof of market. Plaud sells the recorder for $160 against roughly $25 cost of goods and a $250 per year subscription, where inference cost is pennies. He says it makes multiple millions of dollars a month.
- Next he wants an AI smart speaker running a local model on a Jetson or Nano-class processor, with about 12 hours of battery.
- He expects powerful LLMs to run on a watch within 18 to 24 months, citing a Moore's-law-like trend in LLM performance by model size.
- The hardware projects are low-probability for a business but good for learning. He recommends having fun intellectual hobbies, since they may help professionally later.
- On advice, he says people are complex systems, so universal rules rarely apply and his own advice should be taken "with a grain of salt".
- He thinks the best advice comes from testing ideas yourself and from close people who know you well. He cites Peter Thiel as famously not giving advice.
- He turned off Twitter DMs, avoids networking and doesn't take advisory requests.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson explains how he spotted looksmaxing as the biggest niche in male self-improvement and shipped UMax in about a month. He covers building novel products, split-testing angles, viral features, bootstrapping over VC, and the long-term vision of a "Hims for self-improvement" brand.

chunks.heading: How Blake builds around a novel idea
chunks.text:
- Blake's core thesis is that most apps fail to hit even $10K/month because they are a "0.1% Improvement", an incremental tweak on something already tried.
- His examples of crowded ideas: a social workout app ("tried like 100 plus times") and a college marketplace app, which was the first app he ever built.
- His rule: "if something has been tried a lot and failed it's usually not a great sign."
- He builds something truly novel instead. He avoids a 1% improvement on a popular product, and avoids squashing two popular products together.
- Plug AI (originally Rizz GPT) worked because it did new things:
  - pickup lines
  - an AI dating coach
  - a "spice" adjuster for responses
  - screenshot-based reply suggestions
- Blake's usual build pattern is to pick a wedge, ship fast, and test.

chunks.heading: Finding a wedge by scanning social media
chunks.text:
- Blake saw a gap in male self-improvement: men are increasingly lost, and the information they get is neither high quality nor personalized.
- He scanned social media to find the most popular niche for young men. That was looksmaxing, so he entered through it.
- His long-term triangle for male self-improvement has three corners:
  - attractiveness
  - physiology (weightlifting, running, exercise)
  - motivation, discipline and mindset
- UMax sits only in the attractiveness corner for now.
- Looksmaxing is male beautification: skincare, eyebrow grooming and hair care, which women have done for decades. Blake sees it as the successor to the gym-bro movement, which has declined on social media over the past few years.
- He frames it as American self-improvement culture ("if you work hard you can achieve a better life"). That is why the niche resonates.

chunks.heading: Building as a user of the niche
chunks.text:
- Blake says: "build something for yourself."
- He wasn't a looksmaxer, so before building he became an active participant on Reddit, Discord, TikTok and Instagram. He wanted to "think like one of the users."
- Research and development ran in parallel. He designed, built and launched the first version in a little over a month, with part-time help from two people.
- On feature prioritization: with 100 ideas you can't assess them objectively. You either split test them, or you are a user yourself and ask what would make you open the app every day.

chunks.heading: UMax product, launch and growth numbers
chunks.text:
- **Product:** the user uploads one front photo and one side photo.
  - They get ratings: overall, potential, jawline, cheekbones, skin quality, masculinity.
  - They also get a personalized "glow-up routine" of recommendations.
  - They rescan weekly to track progress, and results are shareable.
- **Backend:** a mix of classic ML vision and AI vision models such as GPT Vision.
  - Open-source ML libraries detect things like acne.
  - Vision models handle harder calls like hairstyle.
  - About 100 values are classified, covering acne, face shape and jaw contour. These generate the ratings and recommendations.
  - Example: detected acne triggers a routine with benzoyl peroxide and salicylic acid.
- **Launch:** early December. Blake split tested angles, such as ratings versus the recommendations repository, and doubled down on what worked.
- **Trajectory:** a slow trickle for about a month and a half, then organic sharing.
  - Revenue went from about $10K/day to almost $20K/day within a day, and stayed there.
- **Results after about 3.5 months:**
  - 3.5M+ downloads
  - $1.5M+ in revenue
  - roughly $500K/month recurring
  - about $6M ARR
- **Team:** one founder, then a CTO (full stack and ML), one full-time marketer, and about three full-time and three part-time people.
- **Audience:**
  - about 60% US, 30% Europe, 10% rest of world
  - mainly ages 16 to 25

chunks.heading: Marketing: virality plus going wide
chunks.text:
- "The best way to Market an app is to build an app that people organically want to share with their friends."
- Two routes to that:
  - **K-factor optimizations.** He cites Lapse as a company that did this.
  - **A inherently viral feature.** Package it so people want to share it because it's funny, fun or unique.
- UMax's shareable features are the rating card and an AI-generated "you as a 10 out of 10" image. He declined to name the model, because competitors copy features.
- Blake also distributes everywhere: Reddit, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook.
- He works with social media creators and took some on a trip to Hawaii to make content.
- Users post "glow-ups" organically and reference the app, which drives more sharing.
- Possible next feature: show the user's photo with a recommendation applied, such as cleared acne.

chunks.heading: Handling insecurity concerns and copycats
chunks.text:
- **Insecurity critique.** Blake's view: "insecurities are often just desire for change." They can paralyze, or they can push you toward where you want to be.
  - He points to his own scrawny teenage years, which led him to lift almost daily.
  - Users with bad ratings often email to say thanks, because they now know what to work on.
  - He says criticism comes almost exclusively from people outside the community who haven't used the app.
- **Copycats.** There are at least 20 clones.
  - One competitor tried to poach creators and employees, mass-report his accounts, and call his team scammers.
  - Blake says he won't do the same: "strong moral principles."
  - Despite this, the clones haven't taken much traction.

chunks.heading: Business strategy: expansion, profitability and funding
chunks.text:
- **Long-term vision:** a "Hims for self-improvement."
  - Hims became the default destination for men's physiological health issues.
  - Blake wants a brand people go to for fitness, attractiveness, mindset, discipline and focus.
  - He notes tailwinds from Huberman, Chris Williamson and Joe Rogan.
  - Open question: one app, or several apps under one brand.
  - Beyond apps, physical products such as a UMax skincare serum that people could use daily.
- **Plug AI economics:** reached about $200K/month in revenue, and still earns that. The team judged it couldn't scale much further, so they put it on autopilot to build new things.
- **Funding:** Blake leans toward bootstrapping because UMax is highly profitable.
  - He respects founder-VCs, but is wary of VCs who were never founders and have strong opinions.
  - He has heard stories of investors blocking founders.
  - Being "not beholden to anybody" is a strong position.
  - The main open question is how big to scale the team.

chunks.heading: Working with AI models and their limits
chunks.text:
- **Origins:** Blake first used GPT-3 in October 2022, before ChatGPT launched. Early projects included an AI slide deck generator for school.
- **Moderation:** with Plug AI the APIs often refused flirtatious or sexual messages. His fix was workarounds and less restrictive open-source models.
- **Opinion:** he understands the risk aversion of big companies but doesn't like it, and says restricting models resembles restricting free speech.
- **AGI:** he defines it as a "physical Turing test": swap a friend's brain for an LLM and see whether you can tell.
  - He guesses 2025 for AGI, noting GPT-4 with the right tooling might already be there.
  - He guesses around 2029 for ASI, meaning a model that hits exponential growth on its own.
- **Other views:** he believes consciousness is a spectrum, and says psychologists and philosophers should weigh in alongside ML experts.
- **Work ethic:** he thinks most people work much less hard than they believe, including in San Francisco and tech.
- **HF0:** he credits the residency, about 2.5 months in total, for exposing him to unusually brilliant people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson (Cali, UMAX, Riz GPT) joins a short guest segment to explain how he picks consumer app ideas and grows them. He argues for fleshed-out products over single-function gimmicks, using new technology and trend shifts as idea filters, and testing influencer, UGC and paid channels together. The rest of the episode is other hosts and guests.

chunks.heading: How Blake chooses what to build: new trends plus newly possible technology
chunks.text:
- Blake uses two frameworks to decide what to build. The first is "what are people interested in today and this year that they were not interested in last year" (the trend component). Google Trends is one quantitative input.
- The second is "what products can I build today and this year which I could not build last year." He says his successful products capitalized on trends, but "more than anything they're capitalizing on new technology."
- His advice to a would-be founder: ask what newly advanced models and deep tech now make possible that wasn't possible even in 2024, then build with it.
- Examples he gives of current angles: OpenClaw wrappers, or applying the Claude Code style lexical-search agent to different industries. He says he has a few theses of his own but doesn't spell them out.
- His apps map to trends: Riz GPT (AI dating assistant, now Plug AI) to the dating/"rizz" wave, UMAX (face scan with hair and skin recommendations) to looksmaxxing, and Cali (AI calorie tracker) to the protein/fitness wave.

chunks.heading: Why single-function apps are no longer the play
chunks.text:
- Blake says the opportunity in consumer apps still exists, but it is no longer in building a single-function application like his early products.
- Single-function products can still work as consumer interests shift, but he calls a more sustainable strategy "to identify a very clear problem that people experience that is either unsolved or poorly solved and then build an amazing product around that."
- He says people copy his early success with "super niche specific products" and that this is the wrong lesson.
- Example: if he rebuilt an AI dating assistant today, he would not make a screenshot-in, reply-out tool. He would build a suite covering dating profile optimization (photos), message replies, and date planning.
- He observes that the most long-term successful apps on the App Store, before and after AI, "are usually pretty fleshed out, high quality products. They're not cheeky single function products."

chunks.heading: Product vs. distribution vs. engineering
chunks.text:
- Blake's view: great product still wins and always will.
- His analogy: the quality of the product determines the ceiling of the outcome. Distribution and engineering are what actualize that potential and get the company to the ceiling.
- He treats distribution and engineering as equally important.
- He predicts a world with fewer people who are truly great at distribution than people who are great at engineering, which makes distribution skill scarce.

chunks.heading: Consumer app distribution channels and how to test them
chunks.text:
- Blake says the most popular consumer growth approach is short-form social, built on three channels: influencer marketing heavy, UGC heavy, and paid ads heavy.
- He says they are not mutually exclusive and are often mutually advantageous: working one channel makes the others easier.
- His advice: "try them all," then see what you are best at and what your customers respond to most.
- He calls social media the greatest distribution channel on the internet right now. Founders who grew up on it have a leg up, which advantages younger founders.
- He says there are "many ways to skin a cat" for growth, so no single playbook applies.

chunks.heading: Starting small: the first $100 of marketing
chunks.text:
- Blake launched Riz GPT with limited money. He corrects the "$100" claim to roughly $2,000 total, saying the first $100 of marketing spend was the first that actually worked, and that is what got the product going.
- The takeaway he implies is that early validation comes from finding the first marketing spend that works, not from a large budget.
- He bootstrapped the apps with no outside funding.

chunks.heading: Results and track record he cites
chunks.text:
- Background: studied finance, didn't want to work in finance, built apps in school that failed, then built Riz GPT after graduating to pay living expenses.
- Riz GPT (now Plug AI): scaled to a few million ARR, still around $3M per year in revenue.
- UMAX: built a couple of months later, scaled to a few million ARR.
- Cali: the most successful, about $30M revenue last year and about $6M in the most recent month.
- Combined, he says his apps have over 50 million downloads and about $60M in revenue.

chunks.heading: Building as a young founder, college, and hiring
chunks.text:
- Blake says if he were a teenager starting again he would 100% build consumer software, and he thinks it is still the place to be.
- He gives two reasons younger founders are advantaged: they grew up on social platforms (the best distribution channels), and they have built with AI tools for years and so build faster.
- On college: it depends on the goal. It is valuable for fields like theoretical physics (being in the room with peers), and socially. For a CS degree, he says you're probably better off spending most of your time building side projects, for more economic upside.
- As someone who hires and talks to other engineering hirers, he would pick the CS major who built many projects and got a mid GPA over the one who ground for a high grade.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson explains how he went from a flopped social app to AI apps doing millions a month by spotting macro trends, copying proven organic dropshipping-style distribution, and bootstrapping. He covers problem selection, marketing with UGC creators, removing user friction, and why VC money isn't the bottleneck.

chunks.heading: Blake's path into AI apps and the RZ GPT launch
chunks.text:
- Blake graduated from Tulane (finance major, some CS classes, never really learned to code). His senior-year college marketplace app, built with friends and a CTO, flopped. Of social apps he says: "Social apps are very hard to scale. I do not recommend building social apps, especially if you're a first-time founder."
- After graduating he moved home, was borrowing grocery money from his brother, and needed income. He spotted a niche of people showing off their "RZ" (chat game) on dating apps. A roommate on Hinge kept asking what to say to girls, and it was obvious ChatGPT could answer.
- He searched the App Store and found no apps doing it successfully. He built it by asking ChatGPT how to build it (Swift UI, API calls) and pasting the code into Xcode, in the early days of "vibe coding" before Cursor existed.
- Launch: about June 2023, roughly five months after ChatGPT's release. It hit $80,000 MRR within weeks and about $250,000 a month within three months.
- The app was renamed Plug AI after a lawsuit from a company already using the term "RZ" that had little traction.

chunks.heading: How RZ GPT went viral: dropshipping-style organic content
chunks.text:
- Blake says the app went viral because "we took the dropshipping organic content strategy using these sort of underground influencers, UGC, whatever it may be. We applied it to AI apps."
- He pairs distribution (UGC, creator and influencer content, iterating hooks) with a product built around a trend already visible on social media.
- His marketing summary: identify the correct creators, identify the correct hooks for UGC, create the content, put it out into the world, continue to iterate, and double down on what works.

chunks.heading: UMAX: spotting the next wave and shipping on a new API
chunks.text:
- When RZ GPT flatlined around $250,000 a month, Blake saw looksmaxxing taking over social media.
- He knew OpenAI's Vision API (image analysis) was about to launch, so he built the app first: take a photo of your face, get ratings and recommendations on how to look more attractive. The moment the Vision API dropped he plugged it in and launched.
- UMAX reached about $700,000 monthly revenue within roughly one and a half to two months.
- Unit economics he gives: API costs are marginal; Apple takes 30%; influencers are generally 30-40%; then team costs. Every app he has built has had a profit margin above 30%. At $700,000 a month in revenue, he says they took home over $200,000 a month in profit.
- Product design principle ("inspire action without creating insecurity"): UMAX has a floor rating of 55 out of 99; most users score 70+; a "potential" score is always 5-10 points above their rating; recommendations are mundane (go to the gym, eat less calorie-dense food, wash your face). No mewing, bone smashing or hormones.

chunks.heading: Cal AI: partnering and compounding growth
chunks.text:
- A 16-year-old Zach Yadegari DM'd Blake after seeing RZ GPT and UMAX. After weeks of talking, Zach sent a list of ideas and Blake picked the AI calorie tracker. They built Cal AI together.
- Cal AI was not an immediate hit like RZ GPT and UMAX, but "the ceiling has been so much higher." Per Blake it roughly doubled month over month early on ($50K, $100K, $200K, $400K) and is now at about $3.5 million a month in revenue and over 10 million downloads.
- Pricing: about $20-30 a year (just under 10 cents a day), versus My Fitness Pal at roughly $20 a month for the ad-free version.
- Distribution: working with bigger, more reputable creators. They paid MrBeast between $500,000 and $1 million for an ad, and also work with Alex Eubank.
- Product positioning: the viral feature is photo scanning (about 90% accurate by their testing against a verified food database of images, macros and calories). They also offer a manual food database and barcode scanning. He argues the AI scan is more viral for social promos and removes the friction that makes people quit manual tracking. His framework: "don't let perfection be the enemy of improvement."
- On competitors and copycats: he says there are "hundreds, thousands of copycats" and treats mission-driven ones as allies; his focus is improving the product, lowering cost, and getting distribution.

chunks.heading: Principles for finding and validating app ideas
chunks.text:
- Start with problems you or people close to you experience. Do market research, identify key pain points, look at what other apps in similar industries do, then build for the specific problem.
- Blake's own space is self-improvement, which he has studied for over a decade.
- Use existing apps as case studies. Everything is "open sourced" in the sense that the funnel is visible: download Cal AI or search it on TikTok and you see what the consumer sees.
- Copy-and-adapt works: he says tens if not 100+ other apps making over $100,000 a month rebuilt the experience for other domains (quitting sugar or alcohol, scanning supplements, skincare routines for women).
- Macro positioning: AI created new opportunity in consumer apps and social media made distribution easier, so he argues merging those trends was the key decision versus taking a finance job.
- The ground has moved: basic chat is commoditized, so value sits in narrow, specific applications on top of the models.

chunks.heading: Building skills, hiring and bootstrapping
chunks.text:
- Learning to code: use ChatGPT as a personal tutor, not a copy-paste machine. Ask it to explain concepts (MVVM in Swift UI, backend security, API calls, state management), implement, iterate. Copy-pasting alone teaches nothing.
- He says he IQ tested people he has worked with and found roughly 100 IQ people building successful apps; some baseline intelligence is needed, but beyond that "it's really a problem of agency."
- On fundraising: they have all bootstrapped, with starting budgets in the low thousands, and get VC offers "all the time." His view is that VC suits multi-billion-dollar outcomes, and in this space "the bottleneck is not cash." The difference between $100,000 and $5,000 to start is small, mostly speed.
- He believes founders should learn the core skills themselves rather than start with cash and hire people, in this space: "you're actually kind of shooting yourself in the foot if you don't learn how to do the thing yourself."
- He says App Mafia portfolio apps collectively do over $70 million a year. Alumni of his team, such as people who worked on RZ GPT and his UMAX CTO, went on to found studios or apps doing $10 million or more a year.

chunks.heading: App Mafia course and personal-brand strategy
chunks.text:
- App Mafia (with Alex Slater and others) is launching a course teaching how they ideate, design, develop and distribute apps: over 10 hours of content, priced at $2,500, with periodic new case studies. Launch date Saturday the 23rd.
- Blake says they don't need the money; the course is a lever for personal brand. The proceeds fund operations, videography, the house, events and marketing for App Mafia, and the audience then helps with hiring, distribution and future businesses.
- Reason for doing it now: they get DMs constantly asking for this information and had no economic incentive to spend tens of hours structuring it until deciding to push the industry forward.
- They plan to vlog life in the Miami house (about one hour roughly every other week) to break out of the tech bubble onto short-form platforms.
- Claimed assets and spending he mentions: a $40,000 a month house rental, the appmafia.com domain (about $10,000), and cash purchases of a Ferrari 296 GTS.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A loose, banter-heavy podcast with the App Mafia founders. Blake's useful points: use controversy to gain reach and hiring leverage, focus only on the few funnel metrics that matter, take asymmetric bets, and push through self-doubt. Much of the episode is jokes and lifestyle talk with little durable insight.

chunks.heading: Why Blake leans into controversy and social capital
chunks.text:
- He argues the value of social capital and notoriety is only increasing, and he sees it most clearly in hiring: "The more algorithmic reach and distribution that you have, the higher quality talent that you can attract."
- He posted a reel/TikTok saying he would start being "more of a douchebag on social media." His reasoning is that avoiding controversy is ego preservation: people stay risk averse to protect their image, which blocks the influence they could gain.
- His examples of people who rose through controversy: Trump (via The Apprentice), Andrew Tate, Elon Musk, AOC and Bernie Sanders. Some of it is calculated and some is just who they are.
- He is bullish on Cluely and Roy Lee for this reason. He thinks Cluely's product has a way to go, but "getting a crack team in place is most important," and controversy-driven reach lets you build that team and bigger companies over time.
- Case study: Zach (Cal AI) first contacted him via DM after seeing RZGPT and UMAX organically. Blake had posted an egotistical tweet about UMAX's initial traction (UMAX was his second app). He says inbound like this brings in smart, hardworking, mature people.
