- The group's launch logic for their first product (an education/course offering) is the same trade: sacrifice some social capital and take backlash in return for attention and a following.

chunks.heading: Why software is the opportunity, and the thesis behind App Mafia
chunks.text:
- Blake notes that short-form "entrepreneurship" content is dominated by social media marketing, drop shipping, day trading, meme coins and copywriting. He calls many of these poor long-term industries: zero-sum, heavily competed, low margin, and the money often comes from selling courses rather than running the business.
- His question: why is there no hype around building software? His answer is that it was inaccessible for decades.
  - Ten years earlier, an AI calorie tracker like Cal AI would have meant training custom ML vision models from scratch, needing lots of data and millions in funding, with no guarantee it worked.
  - Even a simple mobile app five years ago meant hiring developers or agencies (generally a bad strategy), needing capital, or having a CS degree.
- Today AI plus infrastructure like Firebase and Supabase means almost anyone "sufficiently intelligent" can build. None of the group has a CS master's or a big dev team.
- The aim of App Mafia is to make building software cool and accessible.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping, risk and "yolo" spending
chunks.text:
- He thinks raising money is wrongly treated as the default way to start. He also pushes back on the idea that bootstrapping means being a solo indie hacker with no team.
- His college experience: he took a Tulane entrepreneurship class that was essentially all pitch decks while he was working on a college marketplace app (which failed). His question was why such classes aren't about "just doing the damn thing."
- He thinks most institutions are built to be risk averse and protect the downside, so people study and analyze far more than they act. He adds that this isn't always wildly inefficient, since it keeps things from collapsing.
- His view of teachers: his own professor ran a drop-shipping tea store doing about $10k a month. Founders who really succeed rarely stop to teach. He did get Walter Isaacson (Elon Musk and Steve Jobs biographer) as a mentor and professor, and Isaacson's best advice to him was roughly "most advice is [bullshit]. Do things, lean into what works, take risk."
- Downside of bootstrapping: every dollar spent comes out of your own pocket, whereas VC-backed companies can take bigger swings. He says the group would still yolo everything into a play they believe in.
- He frames risk as a power law: for a ~$500k influencer spend, the Cal AI team expected to get back at least about $300k, counting direct response plus word of mouth, with upside in the millions. His rule: "whenever we get these opportunities we'll take them 10 times out of 10."
- It took the team a while to learn this. The first example he cites is Alex Eubank: roughly $100k a month on a deal when Cal AI was at about $500k a month, followed within months by a jump to over $2M a month, which he credits largely to Eubank and the influencers that deal brought in.
- On being risk tolerant: if everything burned down, they could lock themselves in a room for months and rebuild.

chunks.heading: Stepping-stone path and the team
chunks.text:
- He says the "work on the hardest problem immediately" advice suits some people but not all. Examples he gives: Elon built Zip2 and PayPal before Tesla and SpaceX, Sam Altman did Loopt and YC before OpenAI, and Steve Jobs sold blue boxes before Apple. Bootstrapping fits this progressive path, whereas taking venture capital carries an implicit expectation of pursuing a decacorn-sized outcome.
- On solo founding: before his first full-time hire he bought into "one person, one billion-dollar company." After hiring one person, "I watched the productivity... skyrocket overnight," and he now calls the solo narrative "a complete scam" for most businesses. His advice is to find cracked individuals and hire them.
- He believes in knowing how to do almost everything without needing to be the best at it. Each founder in the group can code, design and market, which makes it easier to identify good hires. He has seen non-technical founders repeatedly hire terrible engineers because they can't tell a bad engineer from a good or great one, and the same applies to marketing.

chunks.heading: Prioritization and shipping fast (RZGPT as the example)
chunks.text:
- His first successful app, RZGPT, launched as a mess: no reviews, no notifications, the app name on download was "RZGPT-roduction," and API keys were exposed in the front end. It still hit about $80K MRR within 3 days. Case studies were written about it.
- His lesson: identify the core components of the business and let everything else wait. The core is getting people to download, converting them, and giving them a good experience so they stay.
- He sees indie hackers optimizing ASO and tiny design tweaks while stuck around $400 MRR, which is effort on the wrong things.
- As a company grows, the principles you dismissed early (running a tight ship, more process) start to make sense. He compares it to understanding your parents' rules as you grow up.
- Perfectionism and low confidence slow people down. His view is to take life less seriously, accept you'll embarrass yourself and break things, and recognize that more decisions mean more data and stronger intuition. Someone who does nothing never builds mental models.

chunks.heading: Mindset: complex systems, advice and doubt
chunks.text:
- He thinks everyone should study complex systems, because people are complex systems, not single-dimension optimization curves. Two people can take the same actions and get vastly different results, so there are no universal rules. His advice is to lean into your own attributes and strengths.
- He notes that successful founders are very different archetypes, and it is easy to pick three similar ones and ignore everyone outside that pattern.
- He points out that Elon's companies nearly went bankrupt several times. One example he cites: in 2008, when Tesla couldn't make payroll, the investors in the room declined to invest. Elon then said he would do the entire round himself despite having little money, and the room's dynamic shifted so investors wanted in. Survivorship bias hides the identical situations that ended in failure.
- His biggest challenge was doubt. He always felt he had massive potential but had nothing to show for it. By 22 and graduating college he had only worked DoorDash, tutoring, taking tests for other kids and mowing lawns: no internship, no W2, no second-round interview.
- Years of failure followed, even though he was smart, worked hard and took risks. He says most people never get out of that state, but accepting it and pushing forward usually pays off over a long enough time horizon.
- He believes the difference is perseverance, risk tolerance and sacrifice: most people try once or twice half-heartedly, then go back to the standard path. His own freedom framing is that step one is achieving freedom, after which you can go in any direction.

chunks.heading: Future plans
chunks.text:
- He wants to build a Whoop competitor with local-inference AI, is excited about AI hardware and AR software, and does not plan to compete in glasses.
- He sees AR opportunity if and when glasses replace phones as the primary device.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Starter Story visits the Cal AI founders in New York after the multi-million sale. Blake Anderson argues the App Store is still a huge, growing market, that copycats cap out at small outcomes, and that building something genuinely new has far more upside. The transcript has no speaker labels, so attribution is limited to the clearest statements.

chunks.heading: Blake's background and path to Cal AI
chunks.text:
- Blake Anderson is 25 and from Philadelphia. He was co-founder, investor and advisor at Cal AI.
- He began building apps at Tulane. His first apps mostly failed.
- He then switched to building AI apps. After his first two apps, he got in contact with Zach, and the two began building Cal AI together.
- He describes the hand-off as Zach's DM to him, which started the partnership.

chunks.heading: Why a copycat pitch would not have worked on Blake
chunks.text:
- He says copying an existing app and attaching a strong distribution strategy can get you to $10,000 a month or even $100,000 a month.
- He argues the outcomes are much bigger when you build something new, and says he finds that "much more inspiring" on a philosophical level.
- He uses his own story as the test. If Zach's first DM had been "Hey, I created a copycat of this," he says "I wouldn't have responded and we never would have worked together."
- He says many legitimate professionals feel the same way. The people worth building with tend to be drawn to original ideas.

chunks.heading: How big the iOS app opportunity is in 2026
chunks.text:
- Cal AI looks like a huge win (about $50M a year), but he says it was a tiny slice of the whole market.
- The App Store as a whole is about $100 billion a year. Cal AI was roughly 1/12,000th of that total opportunity.
- The market is growing over 10% year over year. He expects it to pass $200 billion in annual spend on the iOS App Store alone within about 6 years.
- Most people picture the opportunity as a fixed pie. He says that once you apply new technology, AI or otherwise, the real opportunity is much larger than that picture suggests.

chunks.heading: Where Blake says to look for ideas
chunks.text:
- Take existing ideas and put a differentiated spin on them. The spin can be different features, a different approach or different distribution.
- He thinks iOS apps will keep getting bigger every year. If he were starting now, building iOS apps is what he would do.
- His answer to "is the app store too flooded?" is yes, the opportunity is still available, as long as the app is differentiated.

chunks.heading: Blake's next project: 10X App Builder
chunks.text:
- After the Cal AI sale he is working on 10X App Builder, which he describes as "Shopify for apps."
- It goes beyond writing code for the user. It helps with ideation, hosts user backends, and helps users design their Instagram page in an aesthetic manner.
- He works from the 10X office. 10X Studio runs there and has several subsidiary companies, and friends' startups share the space.
- He recommends it to anyone who is new to building apps.

chunks.heading: Why he keeps building after a big exit
chunks.text:
- He describes entrepreneurship as a video game he does not want to stop playing.
- His analogy: if you were playing GTA, you would never put your character down and watch TV for 4 hours. For him, entrepreneurship is that game.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Roundtable with the App Mafia founders on running consumer apps (RizzGPT, UMAX, Cali, Quitter) at roughly $50M combined revenue. Blake's contributions cover launching RizzGPT via underpriced niche creators, the three macro trends behind the app boom, low-maintenance apps with one employee, and how to cold DM a founder.

chunks.heading: Low-maintenance consumer apps at 50%+ margins
chunks.text:
- Blake built the first two App Mafia apps, RizzGPT and UMAX. Each does roughly $4M a year, and the wider group (with Cal AI and Quitter) is just over $50M in annual revenue.
- His thesis: "If you build a good product, you don't have to maintain it. The code continues to provide the service on its own." With the marketing system set up correctly, "it'll just continue printing."
- These two apps run at over 50% profit margins. Each has one full-time employee, a social media manager, plus a VA. Blake says he personally does nothing on them.
- Revenue is flat rather than growing, and he reports no churn problem. The apps still run on new downloads: the revenue is "primarily almost entirely for new users."
- The model is subscription (weekly plans are mentioned), fed by continuous new-user acquisition.

chunks.heading: How RizzGPT launched: ChatGPT wrapped as a consumer app
chunks.text:
- Blake first tried a college social marketplace app with a co-founder. It found some traction at his own school, failed to scale to other schools, and fizzled.
- Facing graduation and not wanting a job, he asked "what is the quickest thing I can build that's going to make some money."
- His reasoning:
  - People should be packaging ChatGPT into apps.
  - More consumption happens on phones than laptops.
  - So build a product and market it on social media.
- The product was RizzGPT, an AI dating assistant for guys who can't talk to girls. The user uploads a screenshot and it suggests what to say.
- He expected $10-20K a month, enough to live on while building other businesses. Instead it hit about $80,000 MRR within 3 days of launch.
- The driver was influencer marketing with underground, niche, underpriced creators who had cult-like followings.
- This was the very infancy of the AI app game. Before that, mobile was mostly social apps (NGL, TBH, Gas, Instagram wrapped).

chunks.heading: Three macro trends behind the app boom
chunks.text:
Blake argues the opportunity comes from three forces, and nearly every new player uses at least two, usually all three:

1. **New technology.** There was no major technology shift from the App Store's advent until ChatGPT (2022-2023). Most big apps (MyFitnessPal, Headspace, Calm) date from the early 2010s. LLMs let you embed real functionality into a single-player product.
2. **Easier building.** Previously you had to hire developers, raise capital or be highly skilled. Now you can code with LLMs, and database providers like Supabase are much easier to use.
3. **Dropshipping-style marketing.** It is easy to get a product in front of people through creators.

chunks.heading: Is the app space saturated, and does influencer marketing still work?
chunks.text:
- Blake concedes the low-hanging-fruit AI app ideas have been taken. But "if you have a novel idea there's still plenty of opportunity on the marketing front."
- On influencer competition: it is easy to think more apps means more bidding for creators. Yet the vast majority of influencer promos are for physical products, not apps.

chunks.heading: How Blake responds to cold DMs
chunks.text:
- He shares the example of Zach Yadegari's cold DM, which led with credibility and asked for nothing up front: "I'm a 16-year-old founder and CEO of an unblocked gaming website that has gotten over 4 million users and is monetized with AdSense."
- Zach then referenced Blake's "over 900,000 downloads in 3 months" and asked to learn from a mentor.
- Blake says leading with credibility or value beats a vague ask. Being 16 and already building also appealed to his wish to help younger founders.
- The failing version is "yo bro, thinking about building an app that does this, what do you think?" Blake's reaction: "no chance, dude, I'm not answering that."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a conversation with Cluely founder Roy Lee, Blake Anderson explains how one multi-tool AI product can be marketed separately in each niche, why UX is the real differentiator, and why short-form fragmentation and risk-taking drive outsized wins. Most of the interview is Roy's story. Blake's contributions are shorter asides on distribution and compounding.

chunks.heading: Distribution through a viral hook, with a bigger product underneath
chunks.text:
- Blake and Roy Lee discuss Cluely (Roy's company) and its "cheat on everything" positioning. Blake says Roy's cheating angle works like UMAX's face-rating hook: a viral concept that funnels people into a less viral but more sustainable product.
- Blake says Roy did this before with Interview Coder: start with a narrow "cheat on" use case, then widen it.
- He argues a "Trojan horse" approach is the way to build AI wrappers. Package several single-function tools into one app, but market each niche separately.
  - In astrology, it is "your AI horoscope report."
  - In fitness, it is "an analysis of the workouts you need."
  - In education, it is a cheating tool.
  - Each audience hears about a different feature, and the company underneath is the same.
- He says he wished he had done with UMAX what Roy did: use the hook to get the download, then push people to the bigger product.

chunks.heading: Where AI application companies win: UX and non-obvious use cases
chunks.text:
- Blake thinks the frontier LLMs are roughly the same. In mass consumer products the difference is the UX and how smooth the application feels.
- He cites Perplexity as an example. The labs compete on training foundation models, and Perplexity competed on UX.
- He says memory handling and fast, smooth search are what make ChatGPT impressive. He is not impressed by the idea of a desktop app that just connects to a chat API.
- He says most people do not know what ChatGPT can do or how to prompt it. A blank canvas does not help because people are not that creative. Packaging a specific vertical for them is worth real money.
- He believes the consumer value is context and memory, since an assistant with perfect context becomes more effective as you use it.
- He also believes the key bottleneck today is that you must still explain what you need done. He built a prototype wearable that recorded everything he said and found it very effective.
- He backs the idea of a personal "computing puck" (a Satoshi-style local device). It would hold your personal LLM and memory and connect to the watch, glasses, phone and laptop.
- He is bullish on smart glasses and thinks they could replace the phone.
- He thinks the AI winners in consumer will be the distribution and UX players, not the labs. He sees OpenAI as strongest on the consumer side.

chunks.heading: Personal branding and short-form distribution
chunks.text:
- Blake and Roy agree that the internet forgets. Their examples are Andrew Tate and Donald Trump (who launched a memecoin right after becoming president).
- Blake agrees that attention is the real currency, and that the worst thing you can be is irrelevant.
- Blake says that short form rewards outrageous things, and that distribution is becoming more important.
- He argues Gen Z founders understand distribution and fragmented social platforms in a way older founders do not, because they see the different niches through their friends.
- Blake told a story about xAI. They came to him wanting influencer marketing and short-form virality, and he offered to run it for a few hundred thousand dollars a month with no retainer. They declined and said they would keep prioritizing X because Elon is the most viral person on the platform.
  - His takeaway: engineers do not understand how fragmented social media is. There are separate pockets of the internet, and a post that goes viral in one is invisible in the others.
  - He said back in 2015 something viral was seen by everybody, and that is no longer true.
- He says older founders (over 30) will get "steamrolled by Gen Z" in distribution, while AI labs will keep doing deep tech.

chunks.heading: Risk-taking, compounding wins and the "winners effect"
chunks.text:
- Blake agrees with Roy that risk-taking is positive expected value. His framing: if four in five risks fail at -1, but one in five pays 10x, and you keep compounding, then people see "luck" at the big moment.
- He says most people think risk is bad because they only see the downside of a couple of failures. Meanwhile the people who took none stay at baseline.
- He talks about "winners effect": try 20 pieces of content and all flop, then one hits and the next 10 hit as well. It feels like flow state, and top performers in every field recognize it.
- He says the cause is not luck but a repeating cycle of understanding what works and doubling down.
- Blake's view of success has table stakes: you need to be smart enough and charismatic enough. Past that, it is about choices: taking big risks, making sacrifices, working hard.
- He observes that most people never take big career risks because the downside is a lower position in the social hierarchy.
- He notes that most people are lazy, so working at moderate intensity, sustained, is enough to stand out.
- He says that meeting people far above him in IQ has shown him there is a tradeoff, because some cannot communicate. How far you get is mostly up to how much you push.

chunks.heading: Raising money and building ambitious startups
chunks.text:
- Blake's view of VC: it is a massive lever, and if you are in a competitive space and want to move as fast as possible there is no other option. He has not raised so far because his projects have not been that large, and he likes the freedom.
- He says he will certainly raise in the future.
- He describes why bootstrapping caps the upside. When the money comes out of your own pocket, you cut corners and do not make big bets like hiring someone at $500,000 a year in cash compensation.
- He describes a dynamic where VCs are somewhat predatory to the typical founder, but a founder with leverage (momentum, a hot company) sits in the center and has most of the power.
- He and his partner Zach do not want to work on projects that are not notable or interesting. Some B2B SaaS founders are worth billions and nobody cares about them, and he never wants to be that person.
- He suggests a hiring pitch for a viral company: being a cool place to work, with people around, can beat a bigger paycheck at a large tech company.

chunks.heading: Why people build: biology, status and ambition
chunks.text:
- Blake says his thesis behind every app he has built is that the biological imperative makes the world go around. He and Roy agree that most ambition traces back to primal drives like status and attracting a mate.
- He observes that the people who take big risks are often those who want more control over who they can attract, while others stay comfortable at their position.
- Blake's view of how he builds: "pretty much everything I do is for the sake of women," meaning the products and brands are aimed at that drive.
- He recommends Cartier over a Rolex or Audemars Piguet if you want to attract women, because women recognize it and men do not. He also mentions Van Cleef, and says the Internet Money guys do "female drip" well.

chunks.heading: Mindset: ignore society, know what you want, work hard
chunks.text:
- Blake agrees with Roy's closing point that you can have almost anything if you know exactly what you want, can ignore the voice of society, and work hard. His version: you only internalize it once you are on the other side of the risks (gym effort, hard work, getting yourself blacklisted from the big tech world).
- He says you see what lies on the other side only after you take the risk, and compares it to the allegory of the cave.
- He mentions a mini-sabbatical he is on now, and says that he has been working less hard recently.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Anderson explains how he went from a failed college marketplace app to RizzGPT, UMAX and Cal AI by building on human insecurities and scaling organic creator content. He covers vetting creators by comment-section quality, taking many outreach shots, choosing distribution before product, co-founder equity, and optimizing for learning.

chunks.heading: How Blake finds and validates app ideas
chunks.text:
- He builds around core human insecurities or desires, not around an "overintellectualized use case" he then has to make viral. Examples: RizzGPT (AI tells you what to say on dating apps), UMAX (AI rates your face and says how to become more attractive), Cal AI (AI calorie tracker). Making an over-intellectualized idea viral is, in his words, "a much much harder task."
- Being first to market on a new AI capability is the biggest source of virality. When RizzGPT launched on TikTok, people reacted with "wait, you can have AI tell you what to say on dating apps?"
- He times launches to model releases. He saw the looksmaxing niche growing and GPT Vision about to ship. He built UMAX so he could plug in the API the day GPT Vision became production ready, and launched about 2 days after it hit production-level rate limits.
- Looksmaxing was a tight-knit niche (mostly guys aged about 16 to 24) with almost no monetization. UMAX had "immediate product market fit."
- He thinks one-function viral AI apps were easier in 2024 than 2025. Simple use cases (talk to girls, rate your face, track calories) are taken. Newer viral products are more complex (he cites Cluely, which helps people cheat on interviews).
- He stays at the frontier of AI and moves on quickly. He warns against putting "complete blinders" on for years while ignoring new AI developments.
- He has worked full-time on five projects in about two years: RizzGPT, UMAX, Cal AI, Apex and 10X.
- On whether to stick or quit: many people stay on wrong projects too long, and many quit before a project matures. He asks himself whether he is moving on for good reasons or just wanting new excitement. He cites Speechify, which took years before it took off.
- He avoids copying what everyone else is doing ("mimetic desire"): "you are generally going to get the same results as everybody else." He follows curiosity and optimizes for learning.
- He avoids projects where failure teaches nothing transferable, such as day trading (unless you also sell content or courses about it).

chunks.heading: Distribution-first thinking and pricing
chunks.text:
- He says it helps to know your distribution strategy before building. Engineers tend to ask only "is it technically feasible?" and growth people only "does the channel exist?" He advises understanding both sides.
- His shorthand: study Silicon Valley for product, study dropshipping for marketing. Dropshipping differentiates on how cheaply you can generate views. Silicon Valley puts much more weight on product. The value is at the intersection.
- Distribution channel informs pricing:
  - Paid ads suit a higher LTV and a higher price point, for example $20 a month, or a free trial then $100 a year.
  - Organic suits a lower price point, for example $30 a year or $4 a week.
- The product direction and the distribution channel feed back into each other.
- He applied the TikTok Shop playbook (creators and affiliates making viral product videos) to his own apps. He chose not to move into TikTok Shop because he was optimizing for learning and wanted to stay in AI.

chunks.heading: Influencer and organic marketing tactics
chunks.text:
- He takes many shots. He says if you aren't "DMing hundreds of influencers per day" and wonder why partnerships fail, you aren't taking enough shots. Don't fixate on a handful of names.
- Reach out to every creator whose audience overlaps your target demographic. That is how you learn whether influencer marketing works for your app.
- Pricing: he usually pays a flat rate with a minimum-views clause, for example $10,000 with the expectation of at least 2 million views.
- Watch your target CPM. His example was a $5 target CPM. Some niches cost far more: edtech is expensive, and finance and fintech creators run $50+ per 1,000 views. Find niches that aren't too expensive and check view quality.
- If the app isn't inherently viral, influencer marketing is an uphill battle because you depend on organic recommendation algorithms.
- Early on, UMAX hit $100,000 revenue in month one with roughly 8 to 12 creators (he says "maybe less, maybe like eight"), who had high follower counts and decent views.
- UMAX revenue went from $100,000 in month 1 to $200,000 in month 2 and $700,000 in month 3.
- RizzGPT launched in July 2023 and went from zero to $83,000 MRR in about three days.

chunks.heading: Choosing creators: the comment-section test
chunks.text:
- His main selection metric is engaged comment sections, not follower count or views. History: followers mattered first, then views, and now content quality matters most.
- A video can get a few hundred thousand views in 6 seconds and not convert at all. An engaged comment section signals one or both of these:
  - The creator has a deeply trusting, dedicated fan base.
  - The content is informative or engaging enough that people leave thoughtful replies.
- What to look for:
  - Thoughtful replies and insights, not "a bunch of fire emojis."
  - Top comments with a good number of likes.
  - Sub-replies and conversations. Many comments with no likes on any of them is a bad sign.
  - "You want a community to exist within the comment section."
- He says it isn't a perfect one-to-one mapping, but it is "a very underrated metric."
- Viral views alone are not the goal, because viewers who won't engage in the comments are unlikely to click through to the product.

chunks.heading: Tracking organic campaigns and briefing creators
chunks.text:
- Organic has no platform dashboard, which he sees as part of the opportunity: "If it was easy, everybody would do it."
- His team uses automated spreadsheets. They input video links and track views, likes and engagement over time, then map that to downloads. They also compute median view count, average likes and average comments. Deeper judgment stays intuitive.
- For beginners, he says you don't need heavy tooling. Watch views and downloads over time, and build an intuition for which hooks and creators convert.
- He says good social media marketing comes down to statistics and psychology: psychology for hooks, messaging and negotiating with creators, and statistics for inferring what converts.
- Content brief for every creator, shared as a PDF before they start. It includes:
  - Ways to integrate the product, plus example ideas.
  - Links to videos that did well.
  - Basic stipulations, for example show the product for at least 2 seconds and before the 15-second mark, and tag the brand.
- Creators send the video for approval before posting. He says you can relax this as you scale and trust certain creators.
- The brief saves both sides time and signals professionalism.

chunks.heading: Co-founders and how he structures partnerships
chunks.text:
- He is a big advocate for co-founders. His apps were built with partners:
  - RizzGPT: two co-founders, 3 people in total.
  - UMAX: his older brother (part-time, backend help from a data-analytics job) and Sam Zia, a looksmaxing influencer (part-time at first). Both went full-time after revenue took off.
  - Cal AI: four co-founders. Zach and Henry came to him after seeing his success. Zach gave him a list of ideas and Blake suggested "AI calorie tracker." Jake Castillo joined later as chief marketing officer and fourth co-founder.
- Cal AI structure:
  - Blake, Zach and Henry started with a three-way equal split.
  - Blake acted as coach, providing marketing strategy and capital from earlier ventures, with less day-to-day involvement.
  - Zach covered growth, marketing and design, with some engineering. Henry covered engineering.
  - He says Cal AI will do over $30 million in revenue in 2025.
- His reasoning on equity: an unequal split would have demotivated people, and someone might have left. "It's a lot better to have 50% of a watermelon than 100% of a grape." Great co-founders are "multipliers." Alone, the RizzGPT team might have made $10k to $20k a month; together they hit $250k a month within three months.
- The upside is capped by whether you can capture it, not by your share. Co-founders can also go bad; he has worked with people where it didn't work out.
- Define expectations clearly from the start. The biggest issues come from unclear roles or mismatched ambitions (one wants a billion-dollar business, another wants $50,000 a month). Also address non-delivery on engineering.
- Finding co-founders is hard. He says they usually come from organic relationships over time. Rushing to find someone yields lower-quality candidates.
- A founder split he went through: on RizzGPT he and a co-founder disagreed on product direction and "one of us has to leave." He left, kept his equity and later rebuilt the friendship.

chunks.heading: Opportunities he sees for builders
chunks.text:
- Zero to $10k a month: become highly skilled with AI tools, since the skill applies to design, copywriting, development and marketing. He gave the example of a designer who out-produced nine others in a 2-hour paid test using an AI icon tool.
- Specifically, build and distribute AI-generated content across platforms. If you can generate a few million views a month for a company, you can charge $10k+ a month. He thinks few people do this well. Another version: start a UGC agency and work with app founders.
- App-to-web payments agency: a recent US court ruling lets apps offer web payments. Apple takes 30% (15% for apps under $1M a year in revenue). He and others tested it and see at least a 20% increase in proceeds, and "well over 20%" in his own case. He didn't share the exact number.
  - He says it is an unsolved problem space with many things to test (he has about 10 ideas).
  - His agency idea: offer to optimize an app's web flow for free in exchange for a reference, then source paying clients who pay only if results are good. He thinks an agency could scale past $50,000 a month in profit.
- "Sell the pickaxes" logic: building AI apps has a lower probability of success, but more people overall will make life-changing money from apps than from servicing them. Servicing has a higher chance of success and is less grindy. He cites Cursor and Lovable as servicing companies that became multi-billion-dollar businesses. He builds consumer products because he finds them fun.
- AI hardware (his current side direction): building little devices with his brother using local inference (an open-source LLM on a small processor with SD storage, no network).
  - First project: an AI pocket recorder, built from an ESP32, a microphone, an SD card, Bluetooth and a lithium-ion battery. He cites Plaud as a model: about $160 for the device with roughly $25 cost of goods, plus a $250 a year subscription with inference costing "pennies," making multiple millions a month.
  - Next idea: an AI smart speaker running a local model on a Jetson-class processor. He expects powerful LLMs to fit in a watch within 18 to 24 months.
  - He says the chance of this becoming a business is not high, but he learns either way.

chunks.heading: Principles for taking advice and working
chunks.text:
- Optimize for learning: aim to finish a project with either material success or at least something new learned.
- Do what you find interesting, because it is where you will put in the most hours and creative output. Have intellectual hobbies, since you can't predict how they will help professionally later.
- Treat advice cautiously. People are "very complex systems," so universal principles are hard to create and much general advice doesn't apply. His approach is to test everything and keep what works for you, and to rely on close relationships with people who know you well. He cites Peter Thiel as someone who famously avoids giving advice.
- His own habits: he dislikes networking, turned off Twitter DMs, and keeps a small close circle. He doesn't claim this is advice for everyone, and notes Zach is better at relationships.
- Background: he wrote an ebook at age 9 ("How to Make Money as a Kid"), mowed lawns, and sold candy at school. He also tried dropshipping, Instagram meme pages and Ethereum mining. Earlier ventures made between $100 and about $20,000 each time. Before RizzGPT he built a college marketplace app (with a technical teammate) that made no money. Prototyping the first RizzGPT came from a roommate asking what to message a girl, which he tried in ChatGPT with prompt engineering.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Whop profile of Blake Anderson, who built consumer AI apps (RizzGPT, Umax, Cal AI) with no coding background and grew them mainly through influencer marketing. His quoted interview covers channel mix, app longevity, thinking long-term, and funding Apex at a loss. Much of the essay is the writer's context; only his quotes are used here.

chunks.heading: Cal AI, RizzGPT and Umax: building viral apps with AI and creator marketing
chunks.text:
- Blake's first app, RizzGPT, was built when he had almost no money. His family had run out of funds and his parents sold their house. He moved back home and borrowed grocery money from his older brother. He calls RizzGPT his "last real chance".
- The app lets users upload screenshots of conversations and returns suggested replies, pickup lines and conversation topics.
- He taught himself to code with AI help and no formal training. He spent about 12 hours a day for over a month "just behind the computer coding, only coding". He says he is "not very good at coding".
- He started building it senior year at Tulane, torn between a normal full-time job and building something of his own. He has never held a real job.

chunks.heading: Launching with two $50 creators
chunks.text:
- To launch RizzGPT, Blake found two relatively unknown, underrated TikTok creators and paid them $50 each to make promotional videos.
- The videos went viral overnight, with millions of views and hundreds of thousands of downloads. He did not need large creators to get started.
- Afterward he realized he could repeat the same formula to build more apps.
- His view of the economics: "these businesses don't just die". RizzGPT was still doing about $200k a month.

chunks.heading: Reusing the formula: Umax and Cal AI
chunks.text:
- Umax is a looksmaxxing app. Users upload a selfie, and the AI suggests physical improvements, drawing on beauty standards from around the world and the internet.
- Blake picked a topic already trending among young people (looksmaxxing, rizz) and paired it with AI.
- Umax had made $4.2 million on the Apple App Store alone and was still doing $350k to $400k a month. Apple takes 30%.
- Even after Apple's cut, he estimates that if he stopped working today, the profit attributable to him would be at least $5 to $10 million.
- Cal AI is his third app. Users photograph meals and AI estimates calories.
- Across the apps, he says they still cashflow "a couple hundred" thousand a month, which funds his bigger ventures.

chunks.heading: Distribution: influencer marketing first
chunks.text:
- Blake says the apps grow "primarily by influencer marketing".
- He also runs internal UGC and paid platform ads on Meta and TikTok.
- He uses everything, but influencers are the most profitable channel.

chunks.heading: Tools and the skill barrier
chunks.text:
- Blake works in Cursor, an AI code editor, which he describes as "like an AIDE".
- He taught himself by learning basic sequences, through trial and error, and with more capable AI tools over time.
- His position is that coding experience is not required to build profitable apps.

chunks.heading: Long-term vision over short-term money
chunks.text:
- Blake says he does not think about business as "how can I make $10 million". He thinks about "how I can maximize my impact in the footprint that I leave on the world".
- He says it is "nonsensical to think about money in the short term". You need the resources to build out the long-term vision.
- App profits fund that vision.

chunks.heading: Apex: reinvesting app profits into a community
chunks.text:
- Blake started Apex, a community teaching how to build and market viral mobile apps. It has two courses, App Building 101 and the Web App Blueprint.
- He says he intends to put "at least a few million" into making Apex succeed and had put in about $1 million so far.
- The community is expected to lose about $60k to $70k a month minimum for the foreseeable future, partly because he pays his co-founders a solid salary.
- His co-founders are his best friends from college. Each owns a primary domain and stack, and he wants to transfer lessons from his entrepreneurship to them quickly.
- On risk: "I would rather live at the extreme with a 50% chance that it all crashes and burns."
- He gives money to his parents and his older brother, who lent him money in college.
